subsubtopic: THE POLISH CRISIS-REQUEST THAT PRIME MINISTER SUPPORT SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity, under the provisions of Standing Order 43.
In Poland, suppression of human rights, including the imprisonment of some 50,000 members of Solidarity, seems to be intensifying, and last Sunday, Archbishop Jozel Glemp, leader of the Catholic Church in Poland, said that continued martial law might lead to a "revolt and perhaps even civil war". I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle):
That, in recognition of the fact that nations of the free world should present a united front in opposing martial law in Poland, this House express its disagreement with the ambivalent attitude to the Polish crisis taken by the Prime Minister, an attitude that is encouraging General Jaruzelski and the Soviets to continue their repressive action and is discouraging to the Polish people, since the Prime Minister justified the oppression of ten million Polish members of Solidarity in comparing the situation with his own use of the War Measures Act in 1970; that this House declare the words of the Prime Minister of Canada to be odious and insensitive, and that this House invite the Prime Minister to support his Secretary of State for External Affairs on this matter and that it urge him to seriously consider the evidence obtained by his minister of Soviet involvement in the imposition of martial law in Poland.

EL SALVADOR-IMPACT OF VIOLENCE ON PROPOSED ELECTIONS-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 rise to move a motion under the provisions of Standing Order 43 concerning the forthcoming scheduled elections in El Salvador. In accordance with the resolutions adopted at the Inter-Parliamentary Conference last September, supported by the Canadian delegation, and the recommendations of the Parliamentary Sub-Committee on Latin America and the Caribbean adopted unanimously in December, and in view of the conclusions of the all-party delegation which returned this week from Central America, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie):
That this House strongly urges the Canadian government to withdraw its support for holding elections in the climate of terror and violence which now exists in El Salvador and instead calls for immediate political negotiations to resolve the violence as an essential precondition for elections.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise to move a motion under the provisions of Standing Order 43. In view of the promises made by the government to consult with labour and management in a meaningful way before bringing forward its programs to deal with the very heavy lay-offs which have taken place in the last two years, and in view of the failure of the government to live up to that commitment so that the legislation prepared under ILAP was brought to Parliament without any meaningful input by labour or management, and in view of claims made by labour representatives from both the United Steelworkers and Auto Workers that, so far, the views of the local committees have been largely ignored and that virtually no money spent under the ILAP program has gone to help workers laid off, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans):

subsubtopic: AUTHORITY FOR COLLECTION OF TAXES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I would like to address my question to the Minister of National Revenue. The minister is no doubt aware that to this point in time there is no tax guideline printed and available for employers in this country with regard to the tax changes announced by the Minister of Finance in his budget. On what legal authority do employees of the Ministry of National Revenue instruct or advise employers in this country to deduct from the wages of their employees taxes applied against what may well become taxable, on this day, in advance of the taxing measures being passed by the House of Commons?

speakeroldname: Hon. William Rompkey (Minister of National Revenue):
subsubtopic: AUTHORITY FOR COLLECTION OF TAXES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, specifically under Section 153 of the Income Tax Act and Regulation 101 which expands on that section, it is the duty of the employer to deduct taxes on behalf of his employees. In January of every year the Department of Revenue, as it did this January, sends out tax tables to employers. For the benefit of the Leader of the Opposition I might say that the tax tables this year included the budget provisions of November, so there should be no confusion in the minds of employers. The same tax tables and the same information has been sent to all employers under Section 153 of the Income Tax Act.
While I am on my feet, I might say to the hon. member that I am rather surprised that he raised a question of privilege about an announcement which clarified employee benefits, made when the House of Commons was not in session. I would have thought it important to get that clarification out as soon as possible. Indeed, most workers wanted that. I am particular-

January 28, 1982

ly surprised in the sense that this is beneficial to 12 million Canadians who will see a reduction of their tax through this budget. Indeed, 250,000 people in Newfoundland will improve their financial situation this year as a result of this budget. That was the reason for getting the press release out as soon as possible.
Madam Speaker, is it then legal for an employer to tax an employee at any level he sees fit, or must the employer tax at the legal level as established by the law?

speakeroldname: Hon. William Rompkey (Minister of National Revenue):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, obviously the ways and means motion puts into legality the provisions of the November budget. It is the practice of employers to withhold taxes on behalf of their employees. This is obviously given legal sanction by the ways and means motion through legislation in the House of Commons. It is a time-honoured practice of this House, in fact of all Houses that I know, including the provincial Houses across this country, to operate in exactly the same way as we have been doing for years, including when the party opposite was the government.

Madam Speaker, perhaps the minister is not aware of two facts. First, his own legal officials, in consultation with this party, have indicated that they do not have any legal authority to require employers to collect tax for which there is no legislation. Second, advice being given by the ministry officials over the telephone is that they cannot issue a tax bulletin because there is no legal authority for the collection of the tax. What exactly is the legal authority that allows employers to take taxes from employees in excess of the legal taxes allowed by the laws of Canada?

Madam Speaker, I rise on a matter of personal privilege. For over 14 years I have been a Progressive Conservative, both provincially and nationally. During that period I have had extensive political responsibility, and 1 have thrived on it. With many of my colleagues I dreamed great dreams and sometimes 1 reached so high that I faltered, but always 1 dared to try. Foremost in my mind was the unity of this great nation. On December 2, this assembly bridged 54 years of political failure to give this nation a new Constitution and a new pulse beat. Unity is assured, I am pleased.
However, I have now reached a state of mind where I have lost the desire and even the will to be a Progressive Conservative. The party's vision is not my vision any longer. The party and its leadership have nothing to offer me and I have nothing to offer the party. Therefore, from now on I will be sitting in this assembly as an independent member. I humbly ask, Madam Speaker, that you change my present seating location to a more appropriate one. I deeply thank all those who have travelled the same road as I have over the last 14 years. The journey has been a fascinating and rewarding one.

My question of privilege flows from today's question period, specifically an answer provided to me by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Rompkey).

I refer you, if I may, to Beauchesne's fourth edition. Citation 233 on page 198 reads:
It is one of the old standing principles of our Constitution that the House of Commons should control the Finances of the country. That is the right, privilege and duty of the House. It has been achieved by means of struggle lasting through centuries, beginning from the fourteenth century down to the seventeenth century, when it was fully confirmed, and since then it has never been disputed.
The cardinal principle on which the whole of our financial system is based is that of parliamentary control, and by this is understood not the control of Parliament in its constitutional sense, but control by the Commons alone. Upon this fundamental principle, laid down at the very outset of English parliamentary history and secured by three hundred years of mingled conflict with the Crown, and peaceful growth, is grounded the whole law of finance and, consequently, the whole of the British Constitution.

On two counts I have to interrupt the hon. member. First, the hon. member is raising his question of privilege flowing from the deliberations of this House, and that he can do without notice. As he is exposing the question now, I do have to tell him that because he is not satisfied with the answer of the minister does not constitute a question of privilege.
Further, the hon. member is again discussing the point that he discussed yesterday. At any rate, I have to remind the hon. member that, in my view, the procedure as established by this House has been followed in the sense that a budget has been given to the House and ways and means motions have been deposited following that budget. The process of taxation, which is not included in the Standing Orders, has gone through according to practices which are of long standing.
If the hon. member has a grievance about the way in which the taxes have been collected, that constitutes a grievance but not a question of privilege. The quotation which the hon. member has just read from Beauchesne. of course, refers to the right of parliamentarians to determine and to vote on government expenses. Nothing has changed about that right of parliamentarians. But the particular instance to which the hon. member is referring is covered by the Standing Orders, and as far as the Chair is concerned, the Standing Orders have been followed. I am afraid the hon. member does not have a question of privilege.

speechtext:
that Bill C-88, respecting loans to farmers, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Agriculture.
He said: Madam Speaker, this legislation is extremely important to the farm community and to Canada as a whole. It proposes measures which will strengthen the role of the
Farm Loans
federal Farm Credit Corporation in helping Canadian farmers invest in their industry's future.
When one checks the record, Mr. Speaker, one will find this act has been amended many times since it was first proclaimed in 1959. It was amended in 1961, 1962, 1964, 1966, 1968, 1972, 1975, 1978, and a bill was placed on the Order Paper March 14, 1979, and died there. So when they say there has been no concern about farm credit, history shows how many times the bill has been changed to reflect economic conditions of the day. When you see the increasing amounts of money the farmers needed, how rapidly that escalated as the farm operations became larger and larger along with the increasing value of land, it is a most interesting history to read.
The proposed changes come at a crucial time. Canadian agriculture is on the verge of a new period of development. Of all sections of the national economy, agriculture is the one with perhaps the best opportunity for growth in the balance of this century. The agri-food strategy, which I announced last July, estimated that Canada could increase its output by two-thirds by the year 2000. Both world and domestic markets for agricultural products are expanding. I believe Canadian farmers must and will rise to the challenge of producing for those markets. However, they can only do so provided that we in the federal government do our part to ensure an environment which encourages the necessary investment, and which ensures they receive a reasonable income for their crops and livestock.
To produce food efficiently in order to be able to compete in world markets in the years ahead will require major investments in new technology and new machinery. Some of the new machinery they are working on, for instance in handling forage, will in the next five to ten years revolutionize livestock feeding in Canada. So when we talk about investment in machinery, it is a tremendous investment which a lot of people in Canada do not realize farmers have made. Some machines are used only a few days a year but they must have them to be efficient.
Some farmers will have to expand the size of their farms to achieve the economies of scale necessary to take advantage of modern production methods. They need money to buy land, so it is essential that the Farm Credit Corporation have access to additional funds and Canadian farmers are assured of a constant and sufficient supply of long-term credit.
Why, one may ask, does this money have to come from the Farm Credit Corporation? Why can the farmers not borrow from their local banks or credit unions, as I might if I were buying a new home or seeking funds to start a new business. Why, indeed? One need only look at the record of the banks over the last five years as to how they have handled, or maybe I should say mishandled, farm loans to know the answer to that question. I think hon. members from rural constituencies will agree when I say farmers need a supply of long-term credit from an agency which recognizes the needs of farmers and knows how to lend money responsibly in rural Canada, particularly to the agricultural sector. The Farm Credit Corporation has that kind of knowledge and expertise, Mr. Speaker.

January 28, 1982
Farm Loans
Although I sometimes get letters from individuals who say the FCC has not dealt with them fairly, I think by and large the corporation has a good track record of considering the individual circumstances of their clients and treating them with more sympathy and human dignity than many private lenders have shown in recent months.
In its 22-year history, the Farm Credit Corporation has lent nearly $5 billion to some 160,000 Canadian farmers. Approximately 74,000 loans are in effect at the present time, including 4,328 loans made so far in the year 1981-82. The total amount lent to farmers in the current fiscal year, as of mid-January, was $426.9 million, with the average loan being a little more than $98,000-approximately $100,000.
In the last two decades, the Farm Credit Corporation has been one of the most important factors in helping Canadian farmers establish and expand their agricultural production and increase the efficiency of their operations. The federal government's conviction of the need for a national credit corporation to assist agricultural development has been reinforced by the excellent record which the Farm Credit Corporation has attained in carrying out its function. At the moment, more than 93 per cent of all Farm Credit Corporation loans are in very good standing. We should not forget that these loans are made to people who, in most instances, cannot borrow money from any private lending institution, because that was the intent of the Farm Credit Corporation in the first instance.
In better economic times, the farmers' rate of property payment of these federal loans is even higher. Sometimes less than 2 per cent or 3 per cent are in default or in some difficulty; however, at the present time it is about 7 per cent. We are right to put faith in the ability of Canadian farmers to invest well with the funds extended by the Farm Credit Corporation. We must now make more money available to the farmers through the corporation. I spoke earlier about the number of times amendments have been made to the Farm Credit Corporation, generally for the purpose of allowing the government to lend more money and to provide more capital for the Farm Credit Corporation.
The Farm Credit Corporation was established in 1959. For most of its history, this federal agency has been the major lender for farm mortgages in this country. As recently as 1975, the Farm Credit Corporation extended more than 70 per cent of all the long-term credit needed by farmers. In 1975, the banks extended virtually no farm mortgage credit. At that time, six years ago, I appealed to the banks to get involved in the long-term farm credit market because I saw a need for wider sources of credit. As I expected, the demand for longterm credit in the agricultural sector has rapidly grown in the last few years. The increase in demand for farm credit financing has grown by approximately 20 per cent annually. The banks have responded to this growing demand, and so have the credit unions. Let us look at some figures. In 1980, for instance, credit unions lent $424.4 million in long-term credit to farmers. That was 20 per cent of the total, across Canada,
for farmers. The banks lent $457.6 million, or 23 per cent of the total. The Farm Credit Corporation lent $498.7 million, which was about 25 per cent of the total, nearly $500 million. The remaining amount came from provincial agencies and private individuals.
In many instances, what farmers thought was long-term credit which they borrowed from the banks turned out not to be long-term credit. I believe some of them signed agreements which they did not really understand. Agreements which they thought were mortgages could be turned over into demand notes when that lending institution so desired. In my office I have documented letters which show that some of them were refused long-term credit. The Bank Act clearly states that the banks can do this kind of thing; that is, they can provide long-term credit with fixed interest rates if they so desire, and they have done this in some instances. Many people buy debentures from the banks for long terms. I recently heard from a man in my constituency who sold his farm several years ago. Elis debenture with the bank now yields him 9 per cent on $150,000.
The banks have many ways of raising money, and they have a great deal of money on which they are not paying high interest rates. The Bank Act gives them a lot of leeway to do the kind of job which should be done in the rural, agricultural community of Canada. However, this has not been done in the right fashion, because it is obvious to me that a large percentage of these farmers would not be in financial difficulty if the physical structures which they built, such as new buildings for housing their livestock and feeding operations for both beef and swine, had been financed on ten-year mortgages. They would not be in difficulty now since in most instances they built during the period when the interest rate fluctuated somewhere between 9 per cent and 11 per cent. However, because they had a combination of floating loans and depressed markets for commodities they were selling, when the interest rates went as high as 24 per cent for some of these people, it was impossible to continue to carry on.
The need for economic restraint in federal government spending in recent years has prevented us from substantially increasing the funds available to the Farm Credit Corporation to meet the rapidly growing demand for long-term investments in agriculture. We realize that this is causing a serious problem for many Canadian farmers, especially since the private lending sector, as I said, has not performed as well as it should in the administration of farm loans. As I have said outside this House, I am extremely disappointed in the way in which most of the banks, but not all of them, have handled the demand for farm credit. I had made an exception, because I named one bank as being one which I believed to have the best farm lending program of all, but farmers immediately wrote to tell me that that bank was not so good either. Therefore, it is obvious to me that none of them is perfect. In many cases, they have handled the demand for farm credit in an improper way by extending credit beyond the ability of farmers to repay. Some have forced farmers to take out short-term bank loans at

floating interest rates when, as I said, long-term loans at fixed rates should have been made available instead.
Many lenders have shown neither mercy nor consideration for the future food supply of this country by abruptly foreclosing on mortgages and calling in demand notes. One of the things 1 find to be amazing is that there are cases where a farm has been in a family for four generations, has been built and expanded, with perhaps a quarter of a million dollars in interest paid over a few years to a bank or lending institution, which then puts the farm into receivership or bankruptcy. Many cases are not really listed or registered as bankruptcies, so they are not shown in the figures we use here. The number should be much greater. However, the banks are willing to take a loss rather than give a write-off to the benefit of the person who has contributed by paying high interest rates over a long period of time. No mercy will the banks show to that person, who has generally been deprived of even the necessities of life in order to pay interest payments to the bank over, say, a period of five years or ten years. However, the banks are willing to sell it at a loss to some complete stranger rather than give a write-off to that person who has made such a contribution to the lending institution.
This has been brought to my attention by many farmers. In my experience, only one bank has been able to offer a write-off of part of the loan. It has said that if one can obtain the rest of the money through the Farm Credit Corporation or the Small Business Development Bond, it would go along with that kind of an operation. This is the only instance in many hundreds with which we have dealt.
Nevertheless, the banks do have an ongoing and important role to play in farm credit, and 1 hope they are now looking, as I understand some are, at their farm lending policies in order to improve their future dealings with the farm community. However, there are legitimate credit requirements of farmers which banks and credit unions will never be able to serve because the potential borrower does not meet their security or repayment rules. These farmers, in particular, will benefit from the additional funding to be provided through this legislation which we are discussing today.
The most important amendment being proposed is that a new source of future funding be provided for the Farm Credit Corporation. The bill contains amendments which would enable the corporation to borrow money from the financial markets. A major portion of its budget would still be derived from the Consolidated Revenue Fund; however, the corporation would be in a position to supplement its loan funds from other sources. It is estimated that with an agent of Her Majesty status, under normal interest rate conditions the extra cost of borrowing from the financial market would be between one half and one percentage point above the current cost of funds through the government.
With the authority to borrow from sources other than the Minister of Finance, it is expected that the FCC will borrow in the financial markets through private placements by an agent.
Farm Loans
The debt instruments, such as bonds or debentures, offered by the Farm Credit Corporation would likely be purchased by institutional investors, such as life insurance companies, trust companies, pension funds and other investment companies interested in acquiring high-grade securities for their portfolios.
Farmers, particularly retiring farmers, have often asked me about the possibility of investing funds in the FCC so that they can assist young and beginning farmers. With this proposed amendment, a special investment mechanism could be developed to channel funds from these retiring farmers into the FCC.
A type of investment fund could be established where retiring farmers could invest the proceeds from the sale of their farms. In principle, it could be the same as the current registered retirement savings plans, with a retiring farmer being allowed a major contribution in the sale of his farm. A farm would essentially be transferring his retirement plan, that is the equity in his farm, to a more formal investment.
In the future, consideration could be given to providing special tax concessions on bonds sold by the Farm Credit Corporation. This would effectively reduce the Farm Credit Corporation's cost of funds and permit it to loan at a lower rate to young and beginning farmers, or to those in financial difficulty, for example.
A further amendment set forth in this bill provides that the maximum amount of a loan be prescribed by regulations rather than in the act. That is so that if conditions change, it is not necessary to come back to the House and wait your turn in the legislative line-up to get a bill through.
Currently the limits specified in the act are $200,000 when there is one qualifying applicant in a farming enterprise and $400,000 when there is more than one. It is no secret that financing a farming operation is getting more and more expensive all the time. It is no different from any other business.
If the Farm Credit Corporation is to meet the needs of today's and tomorrow's farmers, it must have the flexibility to adjust the loan maximum upwards when necessary. Some people think that when a farmer spends a tremendous amount of money in his farm operation he must be rich. A recent report in The Globe and Mail, a large daily newspaper in Canada, attempted to show how rich farmers are. I have the complete breakdown by the Farm Credit Corporation. It shows exactly what a farmer's investment is, how rich he is and what his returns are, but that was eliminated from the published report. It was not there.
There is hardly a businessman in Canada who would operate on as slim a margin as farmers. The ordinary person reading that newspaper report would think that every farmer in Canada is rich because of the amount of his holdings. As we know, they do have holdings, but very little capital that they can use.
Transferring the loan limits from the act to the regulations will provide an opportunity for the corporation to respond more quickly to changing agricultural conditions. At this time,

January 28, 1982
Farm Loans
and we hope this bill becomes law quickly, we are proposing to increase these limits to $300,000 for one qualifying applicant and $500,000 when there is more than one applicant. It may be necessary to use regulations to change that before the year is out, who knows?
Another amendment which will benefit FCC borrowers provides the corporation with the authority to disburse up to 30 per cent of a loan on the basis of acceptable security until the mortgage registration and other security arrangements for the loan are completed. This is a common complaint from the farmers. Once a loan has been approved, there may be no funds. He may then have to go to a private institution to borrow the money temporarily at a higher interest rate. Sometimes this is done under very difficult conditions. In most institutions once the lending institution sees that the loan has been approved, they make the loan. However, it is more costly for the borrower. This initial disbursement will save farmers the cost and inconvenience of having to arrange interim financing until mortgage funds are actually extended by the corporation.
The corporation's borrowing authority is currently limited to 25 times its capital. It is interesting to note that the capital was increased from $56 million to $66 million in 1972, ten years ago. The current capital limit is $150 million. By the end of this fiscal year, capital contributed to the corporation by the Government of Canada will reach almost $143 million. That means the FCC will reach its maximum borrowing authority early in 1982-83. It is therefore necessary to increase the capital from $150 million to $225 million to head off a serious depletion in lending funds.
In recent years I have received numerous representations concerning the age limit fixed on the phasing-in program which allows borrowers under 35 years of age to work off the farm for up to five years. Bill C-88 proposes to remove this age limit from the program because it is discriminatory. Approximately 74 per cent of loans were made to those between 18 and 35 in 1980-81.
The second part of the bill will give the corporation the authority needed to rebate five percentage points on the interest for loans under the special farm financial assistance program announced in the November 12 budget. This authority will allow me to obtain the necessary funds through departmental estimates.
The FCC has already made 89 loans under this special program. A total of $11 million has been loaned with the average loans being almost $124,000. As hon. members know, of the $50 million budgeted for this program, $45 million will go to the farmers and $5 million for the interest subsidy. This is for farmers facing the most difficult financial problems at the present time.
It is interesting to see where these applications are coming from. Naturally, the vast majority come from Ontario. Applications in some western provinces are almost nil. The need is not there. It depends on the kind of agricultural production entity that they have. I am pleased that the FCC was quick to respond following the budget announcement and
that it has already processed many inquiries. I am told that by the end of the fiscal year all of that money will be lent, and it better be! I am sure the corporation is doing a very thorough job, as it usually does.
In addition to doing the work on Farm Credit Corporation loans, the corporation has 203 credit advisers in 110 offices across Canada. They are also assisting farmers in making applications for small business bonds from other lenders. With this program the farmer can borrow the maximum $200,000 under the Farm Credit Corporation and the family can get a small business bond from another lender at a reduced rate of interest, fixed for five years. This will give them an opportunity to recoup their position. They will not make that much money unless there is a better marketing system for what they produce. I will touch on that later.
I have only touched on the most important changes being proposed. Many of the other amendments will help streamline the operation of the FCC and I look forward to a full discussion of these in committee.
The hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Wise) pointed out on Monday that this legislation has been promised for sorpe time. I would have liked to have had this legislation considered sooner. However, it is my belief that my officials and I have used the extra time to good advantage to listen to and discuss the many suggestions brought forward by farm organizations. The hon. member for Elgin participated in a program that studied farm financing just before Christmas and I am sure he would not want me to bring in some legislation without hearing the report of that committee before we finally drafted this. I believe we have accomplished some of those things and I am sure the hon. member will tell me shortly that I have not accomplished them all. This is why, for the fourth time, I will have the hon. member for Saskatoon-Humboldt-

I was looking forward to hearing from the learned and experienced member. I will willingly pay attention to the hon. member when he does speak.
I read in the paper that I had not done anything for farm credit in five years. We went back and reviewed the situation. Since I have been minister, there was a bill introduced in 1972, 1975, twice in 1978 and one in 1979 which died on the Order Paper-almost every second year we have done something about farm credit. One gets the impression from the paper that we have not shown any concern for the needs of farmers. I just want to put that on the record.
The amendments I have outlined today come as a result of many letters and personal representations from individual farmers, farm organizations, the FCC advisory committee, provincial ministers of agriculture and my fellow members of Parliament. All have stressed the need for more long-term credit for Canadian farmers. We are not pretending, by any stretch of the imagination, that this bill will be the answer for every Canadian farmer. We still think there is a definite place

January 28, 1982
for the lending institutions to develop a proper lending policy because of the importance of food production. They have just as much responsibility to those farmers who are in financial difficulty, because I suggest they have put many of them in trouble as a result of their lending practices. In fact, they probably have more responsibility to help those farmers out of their financial difficulty than I have as Minister of Agriculture. I asked them to make loans in rural Canada, and as I said earlier, I did not know they would do that kind of job.
This bill will provide more long-term credit for farmers and also strengthen the Farm Credit Corporation's ability to respond to the needs of our producers.
The FCC is helping to ensure that the Canadian family farm remains a stable and viable entity. It is probably one of the most decentralized organizations, as is Agriculture Canada, since confederation, because the vast majority or our employees are located from Nova Scotia through to British Columbia. They are not all here in the capital. These people understand the needs of the farmers in their communities because they work with them all the time. It is said that we have not done all the things we should have done. There is other money being provided to farmers actually interest-free, a fact which many people are not aware of. For instance, we passed the Advanced Payments for Crops Act for crops outside the responsibility of the Wheat Board. I believe it was estimated that we would probably lend $40 million under that legislation. This year we are lending some $136 million in interest-free advance payments to farmers for the lifetime storage of that crop.
If you consider the advance payments on grain under the Wheat Board this year, Mr. Speaker, you will find those interest-free payments amount to well over $300 million. Before the year ends, I think you will find about $500 million has been provided interest-free to farmers. You will also see in this fiscal year that the Farm Credit Corporation will have again lent over $500 million at an interest rate which will average much below the interest rate being charged by other lending institutions for the fiscal year. I would say we will average at least five points below what other lending institutions have provided for the whole year.
1 urge hon. members to show their support for Canadian farmers. The House leaders have already come to an agreement on the number of days for debate of this bill before it goes to committee.
Again, I urge hon. members to show their support for Canadian farmers through this legislation, and if they have other sound recommendations, I am not beyond accepting them when the bill is before committee or when it comes forward for third reading in the House if the recommendations are practical and improve the legislation. I urge hon. members to show their support for Canadian farmers by improving, through this legislation, the farm credit service provided by the federal government so it is what we want it to be. Indeed, I cannot imagine a man or a woman among my colleagues, regardless of where they sit in this House, who would not
Farm Loans
support the farmers at this vital point in the agricultural industry by denying them this worth-while legislation.
I want to conclude by saying that the government, and I am sure the Farm Credit Corporation, would be irresponsible if we were to lend money carelessly. A large percentage of the people-some 95 per cent of them-who are in trouble are in the red meat industry in Canada. The other 5 per cent are from the horticultural sector, with a few in the dairy sector who borrowed money from a lending institution outside any provincial lending institution or the Farm Credit Corporation. They borrowed it thinking they had fixed interest rates and so on, and then when their return was about 10 per cent on investment and their interest rates went up as high as 24 per cent, they were just not able to carry on.
So what I am saying is yes, we can make the Farm Credit Corporation a better institution, we can help the Farm Credit Corporation people to do a better job-a job we all want to see them do-and people who are in financial difficulties will be unable to repay their mortgages unless they have better marketing facilities and we are able to guarantee them a better economic return.
I look forward to hearing what the next speaker has to say.

Probably one of the reasons that the repayment rate under the farm credit program is right now in default in about 7 per cent of its loans could be that the criteria which has been established for lending under the Farm Credit Corporation is a little stiff, a little heavy. Perhaps we are not taking enough of a chance on young or new farmers, men and women who wish to enter the agriculture field. Maybe that is one of the reasons. The minister knows, and I know, that the other reason is that

January 28, 1982
Farm Loans
people involved in the agriculture industry attempt to maintain a credit standing because credit is so necessary in the production of food in Canada. It is becoming more a part of production every day.
We wonder about the delay of this bill. The minister said he felt the time had been put to good use and that the delay had not affected the bill negatively but had strengthened it. I think that could be debated because since 1979 this is the only time we have had an opportunity to debate a Farm Credit Corporation bill. In 1979 when my colleague, the hon. member for Elgin, was in charge of the Department of Agriculture and the Farm Credit Corporation, $50 million was provided for additional farm credit lending. We had hoped that in 1980 there would be an additional $100 million. In 1981 there should have been an additional $150 million. In 1982 there should be an additional $200 million just to keep up with inflation and rising land costs all over Canada, and I am sure those costs will continue to increase.
I hope the government does not consider borrowing from the marketplace is the panacea or the only answer. I see that the minister agrees. I believe he is sincere in that, and 1 hope officials of the Farm Credit Corporation will increase pressure for additional funding from the federal treasury. However, there should not be federal funding if it is not necessary. The Farm Credit Corporation is anything but a granting institution. It lends funds to the agriculture industry and is repaid with interest. The corporation does not give money to producers. In times of financial difficulty and when there is pressure on the government, it may be that the government might decrease funding for the Farm Credit Corporation or fail to keep funding at inflationary levels. We have faced high inflationary levels in Canada over the last few years and will continue to face them in the next few years under some of the policies we see presented. When the Farm Credit Corporation bill, Bill C-88, goes to committee, I hope the minister will assure us that the federal government will not relinquish its role in financing farm credit and that he will put something into the law which we can accept as a guarantee that farm credit will continue to be funded by the federal treasury at least at the level of the inflation rate in the Canadian economy, and hopefully higher, and at the rate land prices increase throughout Canada.
Sometimes we wonder about the minister. He has stated he is very pleased to be able to do this, but it is interesting that according to the London Free Press of January 31, 1980, the minister said he would not allow the Farm Credit Corporation to receive funds from outside because that would create privatization of the Farm Credit Corporation.

Some of the other issues hinging on Bill C-88 are some of the promises made during the 1980 election campaign, and I hope the producers involved will not have to wait as long for those promises to be fulfilled by the Minister of Agriculture as they have had to wait for Bill C-88.
Credit is a necessity in the farming industry. It is important that everyone in Canada understands that about 15 per cent of the costs paid out by the agricultural industry is for interest. Right now 15 per cent of the cost of production is made up of interest payments in one form or another. Credit is one of the biggest problems farmers in Canada face today, and the cost of credit is continually rising. I hope the next time we look at farm credit the minister will not be increasing the rate of interest borrowers will have to pay to the Farm Credit Corporation. I hope he will be able to decrease that rate.
In 1979, $634 million was made available to the Crown Credit Corporation. I think there were some unusual circumstances that year. Farmers paid off some loans, which gave the corporation a little more money to lend out. However, from 1979 until now we have not seen an increase which would come anywhere close to maintaining the corporation's ability to lend at the 1979 level. I think the minister would agree that in some areas 30 per cent of the cost of production is interest costs. I refer here to cash crops. The Farm Credit Corporation will be called upon to lend more and more money as time progresses.
Perhaps one of the reasons farmers in western Canada are in a better financial position now is that the minister spends most of his time in Ontario rather than in western Canada. I think that probably speaks for itself. The other thing that might be to our advantage is that the red meat industry does not finish livestock in western Canada. The red meat industry finishes livestock in Ontario. Steps can be taken and should be taken to assist producers in the red meat industry. I do not accept the argument of the Minister of Agriculture that a national marketing board is the panacea for the red meat industry.
I would like to talk about the province of Saskatchewan. Statistics show that operating expenses in the province of Saskatchewan in 1976 were $966 million. In 1980 they were $1.58 billion. The percentage increase between 1976 and 1980

just four years-was 63.6 per cent. In 1976 farmers made interest payments amounting to $131 million. According to preliminary figures for 1980 that figure was $285 million, an increase of 117 per cent in four years. Let me compare total farm expenses with total farm cash receipts in the province of Saskatchewan. In 1976 cash receipts were $2.3 million. The preliminary figure for 1980 is $3.13 million. That is a 39.5 per cent increase in four years. However, net farm income decreased by 47 per cent in four years.
It is not that the government has sat idly by. This government has established interest rates which are costing producers in Canada. They are not assisting producers, so I do not think the minister should be so pleased to come in with a small piece of legislation because the legislation has been necessary for the last three years, and hope to see more legislation in the future.
January 28, 1982

I would like to refer to the budget of November 12, 1981. A lot of credibility and enthusiasm was developed by the Minister of Agriculture with an input of $50 million for farmers in dire straits or farmers who were in financial difficulty. Out of that $50 million, only $5 million is available to subsidize interest rates for farmers in financial distress. Those farmers have to be in the position that they cannot even get a small business bond. It is probably 20 per cent of what was necessary, maybe only 10 per cent, or perhaps it was put in without a great deal of thought. When you look at the number of farmers it would really help, you see that the number is negligible.
The Canadian Federation of Agriculture has said that the Farm Credit Corporation provision is disgracefully inadequate and is a sop to the requests of farmers for some real help. It points out that the $45 million provided in the budget allows only $100,000 for 450 farmers. Yet a farmer needs $200,000 minimum today to start up a farm, so that assists only 225 farmers.
I have some questions about how the minister's food policy will be developed when we do not have enough government assistance to enable people to become involved in agriculture. Even with this financial provision there is not enough financial assistance to transfer land from generation to generation or from individual to individual.
I hope that the refinancing of the Farm Credit Corporation by the private sector will work. I wonder if the Minister of Agriculture could persuade the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) or the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Rompkey) to allow individuals who have retired and have sold their farms to place money in the Farm Credit Corporation with the same benefits that the government has given to the banks to lend money out on the Small Business Development Bond, where the banks do not pay tax on the interest received and where the individual does not deduct it from his tax when he borrows money. We know that the producers who find themselves in financial difficulty are not in a position to pay tax; therefore the cost to the federal treasury would be nil. Hundreds of Canadian farmers who are retiring would be pleased to place funds at the disposal of the Farm Credit Corporation in order to help other farmers come back into the industry.
In the province of Saskatchewan the average age of the farmer is 50 and the average age of retirement is 57. There are a lot of people who are no longer interested in, and in some cases are no longer capable of, carrying out the business of , farming who would like to be able to transfer their land. With tight money and the high interest costs on other sources of financing, they are unable to do this.
I am sure the minister would agree that the changes made in the budget of November, 1981, regarding income averaging annuity contracts have frozen the land sales of this generation. Until there is some change in the capital gains tax and until there is some change in the ability of individuals to use the
Farm Loans
funds they have saved or the capital from their farms that will protect that from exorbitant taxation at the time of sale, this generation is going to have to continue to maintain control of the land. As a result, agriculture will not prosper when people would sooner retire from the business and have younger men and women take their place.
There is an option in Saskatchewan-but it is not a very good one-called the land bank, where the government buys the land from the retiring farmer. The government contends that this is a good plan because it offers the land back to the farmer in five years. In one instance, however, where the government bought the land for $100 per acre it offered to sell it back to the individual in five years for $400 per acre. The minister should consider such cases because due to the lack of funding by the Farm Credit Corporation some individuals in Saskatchewan are forced to sell to the land bank. The land usually remains in the hands of the government because it insists on recovering a profit of 400 per cent within five years.
1 hope that the changes in the Farm Credit Corporation will assist individuals who are having difficulty transferring farms from generation to generation. Individuals who are asked about the treatment they receive from the Farm Credit Corporation say, in almost every instance, that it is good, fair and reasonable. I do not think that is due to the Minister of Agriculture as much as it is to a lot of the people in the field, such as the Farm Credit Corporation advisers. I hear it filters down from the top, but if that were the case I think some farmers would be in greater difficulty than they are now. I should like to commend the men and women who work for the Farm Credit Corporation for the service they give to people in the farming communities of this country.
I should not like to end on a negative note, Mr. Speaker, so 1 should like to put a few questions to the minister. I am sure he has heard them before but we have not had answers to them. Perhaps his parliamentary secretary, who is very capable and 1 am sure is of great assistance to the minister, could answer some of them.
We requested that a moratorium be placed on farm bankruptcies and we wonder why the minister has not taken any interest in this request. We do not think it is an answer to the problem but we think it is a way to save the farm in tough times. I am sure the minister would like to answer that question.
We also wonder why the Farm Credit Corporation was given $50 million in November, 1981, rather than $500 million. We also wonder why the Small Business Development Bond is administered solely by the banks. I have heard the minister express some feelings about the banks so I thought he would be the last person to place this matter in their hands. Why could it not be placed in the hands of the Farm Credit Corporation? It could issue the Small Business Development Bonds, especially in view of the changes we are discussing today.
I am sure the minister is familiar with the agri-bond concept and the proposal made by the Ontario Federation of Agriculture which wanted a market insurance risk plan. That sugges-

January 28, 1982
Farm Loans
tion may not be the answer to the problem but it is something that would give assistance and add stability to the agricultural sector.
There are subsidies for all kinds of things all over Canada, Mr. Speaker, even in other areas of agriculture. We would like to know why there could not be a short-term or medium-term loan subsidy on interest rates.
It is also important to know what happened to the promise of the Minister of Agriculture on valuation day concerning the re-evaluation of capital gains. I distinctly remember the minister saying that it would be moved up to 1974. This would have helped, but he needed something else during the election campaign to entice votes from farmers. He said that he would give them a once-in-a-lifetime exemption from capital gains tax. That was a promise of the Liberal campaign, a promise of the Minister of Agriculture. Now we see what happened. Not only has valuation day remained unchanged from 1971, one of the years in which land was at its lowest price in a long time- it has not been changed to 1974-but there is no once-in-a-lifetime exemption from capital gains on farm land. There is no moratorium now, and there are still producers in the agricultural industry who are faced with forced sale prices. It is bad enough that the election promises were not fulfilled, but now we see men and women who have worked for a long time to build up their retirement stakes being taxed by the government under the budget of November 12.
I am sure the minister would like to see these changes. I hope he is successful in making them. The people of rural Canada, whether in the Atlantic provinces, central Canada or western Canada, need those changes if they are to retire with dignity and to pass along their farm land.
In 1979 there was an energy tax credit which would have assisted farmers in the production of food. It would have protected them to some extent against the increased cost of fuel used in production. This would have gone along with the 1979 increases proposed by the Progressive Conservative government, not the exorbitant ones proposed by the Liberal government which are being implemented immediately.
I notice that the minister talked about RRSPs in his speech. He will recall the proposal of the then minister of finance in the December, 1979, budget that there would be $100,000 for people to put into RRSPs; those RRSPs could have been put into farm credit now. The minister spoke of an investment of that type. It is something we look forward to seeing.
I hope I hear the answers I requested from the government side when the turn rolls around to them again, but in closing I should like to refer to the farm bankruptcy statistics between January and October, 1981. In the province of Nova Scotia there were 3; in New Brunswick, 3; in Quebec, 45; in Ontario from where the Minister of Agriculture comes, 126; in Manitoba, 12; in Saskatchewan, 18; in Alberta, 15; in British Columbia, 8, for a total of 230 bankruptcies. Those are 230 families, individuals, men and women, sons and daughters who worked to try to produce food for Canada and to contribute to
our national good. They tried to do something on their own, but we have let them down. I say "we" because there must be some co-operation among hon. members of all parties in the area of agriculture. The agricultural industry is so important to Canada and to individual families that we cannot allow something called politics to destroy Canadian farms.

Mr. Speaker, it is with great pleasure that I rise to speak to the amendments to the Farm Credit Corporation Act in Bill C-88. We have awaited this group of amendments for a long time. I am not sure why we have waited so long because in essence the amendments make the bill more general than it was. They allow for administration of the bill by means of regulation rather than by specific requirements in the bill itself. It loosens up the administration of the bill considerably. Therefore I fail to understand the argument of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) in his presentation as to the excuses for delaying the bill until after he had heard from one task force or another. They were excuses for delay so that he would have a so-called perfect bill, when in fact the bill is so general that it could have been written almost any time. It would apply to almost any day or age simply by the use of the regulations which are pertinent for that day or age.
I am somewhat disturbed by the minister's presentation of the bill. I feel he almost ignored the problem. Granted, he is dealing with a need for farm credit, but he has not been addressing, either in his policy statements and speeches across the country or in the House, what I consider to be the real problem in the area of farm credit. It is not a problem of inadequate credit. Probably more specifically it is a problem of a lack of adequate net incomes in the farming economy because of a lack of attention to other aspects of agricultural policy.
In order to finance agriculture adequately in the short run and to finance the reinvestment requirements of the industry to keep it up to date, net incomes in the long run must be adequate. The industry should be almost self-financing. It has seldom been, but it should be. When we look at net farm income figures, the outstanding farm debt, the value of farm capital, the cost of interest, and at the tables of Agriculture Canada, we see that from 1974 to the end of 1981 there has been very little change in realized net incomes in the country. They were $3.5 billion in 1974. In 1980 they were $3.3 billion. In 1981 we expected to make a little jump up to $4 billion, but the outlook for 1982 is that they will be down 15 per cent or 18 per cent. Basically net farm incomes have remained stable in a time when the value of the dollar has been eroded by more than half. In real terms, available net incomes to farmers are probably half what they were in 1974.
In order to overcome that shortfall, farmers have taken the only available route. They have done the only thing they could do to survive in business. Some of them have failed, but they have attempted to borrow money to make up the shortfall. The farm debt in 1974 was $6.9 billion. At the end of 1980 it was
January 28, 1982

up to $16.6 billion. In an effort to overcome the shortfall in net incomes, farmers have increased borrowings at a phenomenal rate. Because of other policies of the government and I suppose of this continent-because it is a copy of what is ongoing in the United States-along with increased borrowings and high interest rates, we see a very disturbing story of the cost aspects of farming with respect to interest.
In 1974 the total interest paid by Canadian farmers was $473 million. By the end of 1981 it is estimated to be $2,168 billion, which is something over five times as much just in the course of seven years. This was not the minister's expectation, if you go back and look over some of the speeches he has made regarding farm credit and farm income. I do not think he expected that. I think it is indicative of the kind of assessment which the minister has made of the problem. That has very much missed the mark on a solution.
For instance, the minister seems to have got it into his head around 1977, perhaps before, that the way to get out of this problem was not to attack directly the marketing problems that exist in Canadian agriculture, not to attempt to improve the stabilization program so that farm incomes could be maintained at income levels where farmers could refinance themselves, but rather to privatize the lending institutions, open up the banking system and thereby encourage the banking system to take up the slack.
On October 25, 1977, in a speech to the Canadian Bankers' Association at the Chateau Laurier, Ottawa, which was at a time when the minister was looking for something from the banks and not taking a very hard stance with them, he said:
1 take my hat off to banks and other interested financial organizations who are starting to get involved in long-term agricultural lending programs because 1 welcome progress. And this is progress.
That is what the minister said in 1977. In this connection he said that the annual amount of credit used by farms ranged from a possible $9 billion to $12 billion by 1981. The minister saw increased need for credit. He went on to say that he could not see the Farm Credit Corporation taking up that slack.
In fact, the estimate of credit needs was quite a bit off the mark. Instead of being $9 billion to $12 billion, it exceeded $16 billion by the end of 1980. We do not know what the figure is for 1981. Needless to say, no one expects it to be between $9 billion and $12 billion. The minister did encourage the banks to get into the market.
The minister had some rather harsh words in September, 1978, regarding the role which the Farm Credit Corporation was playing up to that time. Agriculture Canada on behalf of the minister issued a news release on September 28, 1978, which reads:
The Farm Credit Corporation is on the verge of being freed from the control of civil servants who don't know about farming. Agriculture Minister Eugene Whelan said Thursday.
Yet we have before us a bill that frees up the role of Parliament and presents to this House a generalized bill, and through it all of the decisions will be made by regulation. I
Farm Loans
suppose from the minister's attitude toward civil servants that the regulations will be written and proposed to cabinet totally by the minister, but I doubt it.

speechtext:
The minister says that he will be listening to our representations.
Generally speaking, we have no major objection to the presentation of this type of bill. We understand that most of the governing of the country is done by regulation. We just do not appreciate the length of time being used as an excuse for slowness in introducing this bill. I think that such a generally worded bill could have been presented to the House much sooner. It changes very little. The actual changes are completely unknown to us. We will have to dig them out when we are in committee and watch for future announcements.
I return to the 1978 press release because it goes on to quote the minister as having said:
-he tried to get the change made when John Turner was finance minister but it wasn't until Jean Chretien took over last September that approval was given.
Now we have approval. That was the basis of the 1978 announcement. Approval may have been given, but the bill has wended its slow and tortuous way to the House through this process and has finally arrived. Although it has gone through a long, tortuous process, we welcome the fact that it has finally arrived.
It is hard not to make any comments about the slow process in light of the minister's attitude toward civil servants getting things done when it took the minister over four years to do something. Instead of carrying on with his self-image of being lean, mean Gene, we should more correctly start referring to him as "glacier Whelan". Glaciers make very imperceptible movements, which is what this ministry and certainly this bill have done.
We in our party have assessed the situation that faces Canadian farmers and Canadian agriculture to be somewhat broader than a need for more credit. While more credit is part and parcel of the immediate solution to turning the situation around, we think that the basic problem is still one of inadequate prices brought about, admittedly in part, by the kind of world pricing situation facing agricultural products all the time. Some things we can do something about and some we cannot. There have been a great many attempts by different nations to combine action, to set up what are sometimes called cartels, other times called agreements, and yet at other times called interstate arrangements, so that the problems of shortages and surpluses can be worked out between nations. At any one time in the world there is usually no great amount of surplus food. Surpluses and shortages occur in certain countries and certain regions.
With the right kind of co-operation, perhaps some day the world will establish a means of communication and transportation that will create pools or banks of food so that countries suffering from shortfalls will be able to draw from those banks. In the meantime, we note the slow progress that has been

January 28, 1982
Farm Loans
made in this regard. However, within the confines of our country there are certain things that can be done. For example, we can examine methods of improving the system of marketing so that farmers who produce the basic product are able to extract maximum returns from the marketplace. Very few of our commodities are structured that way, in part because of some of the difficulties arising from the British North America Act where jurisdiction over agricultural products is shared between the provinces and the federal government. So there has been and continues to be very real and jealously guarded jurisdictions. However, that has been overcome on a number of commodities and I think more effort should be made on those commodities that are not yet in a system of national marketing.
Along with the setting up of agencies to enable producers to extract the maximum return from the market, we have to be aware that, since prices are affected by world market conditions, some form of price insurance or price stability has to be provided agriculture if it is to be self-financing. I think improvements to existing stabilization programs are definitely required if Canada's agriculture is to continue to progress and recapitalize itself to face new challenges.
We have varying forms of crop insurance to cover natural disasters, which I think works moderately well. We should continue that and make certain it is updated to meet the full cash costs of production for those farmers in the position of losing a crop due to sudden weather changes. So we are saying that we do need an aggressive attack on the real problem, the price question which faces agriculture.
The need for credit is peripheral to that. We would not have a large shortfall of credit were there adequate incomes in the first place. However, because we are in this position and it will take a number of years to get ourselves out of it, we have been proposing over the last number of years, certainly since I have been in the House and I know my colleagues here before me have made similar suggestions to previous governments, that there must be a method whereby our agricultural resources can be turned over from one generation to the other, which method is self-generating and self-financing.
We have said on many occasions that there are some moves which this government could make to facilitate this. 1 wrote to the minister and the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) prior to the budget on a number of occasions, outlining suggestions to improve the credit position of farmers. These included a form of bond that would allow the retiring farmer to reinvest his money in farm credit bonds or some similar instrument, with the co-operation of the Department of National Revenue. We think there could be a great pool of funds developed for refinancing farm land by deferring the capital gains tax on the sale of land until such time as the retiring farmer has to withdraw his funds from the FCC in order to meet his retirement income needs. This would mean that the agency could have the use of that money for about two thirds or three quarters, probably two thirds, of the current interest
rate. This would be useful and acceptable to the retiring farmer and would make a great deal more money available to the beginning or expanding farmer. It would not cost the government anything except a little bit of deferred taxes, and would be a very useful and obvious pool of investment capital.
Added to that could be a program allowing farmers with particularly high income years to invest in that kind of bond on a similar basis, which would make further funds available to the FCC at much below market rates on the understanding that tax on that income could be deferred until drawn out for use by the individual. Neither of those options has been taken up; instead the government chose to present a bill which leaves the option open, but we do not know if it is there.
We wish there had been some announcement along with this bill outlining the government's intentions regarding the regulations, and where they intend to get the funds mentioned in the bill. I think we will be pursuing that in committee and 1 hope the minister and his officials will be prepared to discuss those questions there.
Without taking up a lot of the time of the House on this particular bill, I am going to attempt to review my impression of it so that we can go on to complete the debate as quickly as possible. As I said, this bill has been talked about for four or five years, both by this minister and the previous minister in the Conservative government. Some of the original reasons for presenting these kinds of amendments seem to be changing as the minister changes his mind about whether the banks are good guys or bad guys. However, we still have the opening, the way this bill is written, for banks to take over an even larger chunk of Canada's farm credit needs.
Those needs are not unsubstantial. As I recall, the banks are filling about 30 per cent of the total requirements, most of it on a short-term basis, along with a goodly chunk of the medium-term capital required. This bill appears to increase the capital available to the FCC so that they may now have up to $5.6 billion outstanding, up from $3.75 billion, or roughly a 50 per cent increase. From the way the bill is written it is not clear how much of that will be available soon or from what source. We do not know how much is private money or how much is public money. This kind of basic information is not available to us in the bill. I hope the minister and his officials will be able to give us some indication of that when it gets to committee.
Because we do not know the relationship of public to private money, it is very difficult to get an idea as to what kind of interest rates there will be. If we do go out strictly on the public market without using any of the provisions I have discussed in my presentations to the minister and to the Minister of Finance, I do not see how the public money will be able to reduce interest rates to the Farm Credit Corporation. The government may have a magic formula, and I would be very interested to hear how that particular program will work to bring about lower interest rates.
January 28, 1982

In fact, an interesting altercation took place on the radio noon show today. George Price the farm broadcaster, while hosting an interview on this very subject, asked a very fundamental question, namely, whether interest rates will continue to rise. One of the civil servants who had been identified as a vice-chairman of the Farm Credit Corporation, Paul Babey, began to say yes, but the minister interrupted to explain that they will not be rising. We will be interested to find out the various points of view concerning that matter when it gets to committee, as well.

Well, it is not certain. My colleague asked whether the minister is in charge. It is not certain just who is in charge at the moment. He was not going to leave it up to the civil servants, yet the bill seems to leave a great deal of it up to the civil servants.
We agree that the corporation should be increased to seven members. We support this move. Also, we have no objection to the ceiling on eligibility for loans being set by regulation. We think this will allow for more flexibility and will probably allow hon. members of this House and farm organizations to have as much leverage in decisions as we would if such matters went into a bill and were locked in for several years before the bill could come back to the House. We have no objection to that.
While I am standing, I wish to make note that it seems that some changes and broadening of the regulations have been made as they apply to Indian bands. There was formerly a ceiling of $400,000 on loans to Indian bands. Now this ceiling will not be set in the act itself but will be subject to regulation. I hope that regulation will make that ceiling a great deal higher so that Indian bands with substantial agricultural land to develop can take advantage of Farm Credit Corporation loans to do so.
I also note that, while there is only one mention of agricultural production co-operatives in this bill, and a similar kind of notation would be made by the minister and his officials, some production co-operatives need great amounts of capital, too. As long as co-operatives are operated by their members and shareholders, when regulations are being drafted consideration should be given to that aspect of agricultural production as well. It is a kind of agricultural production which is very often forgotten in regulations made here in Ottawa. I hope when it comes to making Farm Credit Corporation funds available that that form of agriculture production will not be ignored.
1 note that there will be some changes to the regulations and to the bill itself with regard to age limits on farmers. I would just like to take a moment to congratulate the hon. member for Selkirk-Interlake (Mr. Sargeant) for his work in getting the ceiling lifted on age 35. This was done through his discussions with the Human Rights Commissioner, Mr. Fairweather, who noted, upon reviewing the matter, that this was indeed a discriminatory clause. I think the intervention by my col-
Farm Loans
league, the hon. member for Selkirk-Interlake, had a great deal to do with the change in this part of the act.
Another aspect to this ceiling of age 35 in the bill is that a bit of sex discrimination was beginning to emerge in the Farm Credit Corporation as well. I hope the particular wording now contained in the bill will eliminate that. There were a number of instances where, because of the age 35 ceiling, a wife would make an application as the farmer and owner because she happened to be under age 35. In a great many of these cases there was much difficulty in convincing various officials that females could be farmers. I hope this aspect will disappear from the act as a result of this new wording and that it will not show up again in the forthcoming regulations.
In conclusion, I would just like to reiterate my initial comment that the farm income situation looks very grim. It is projected that in 1981-82 incomes will drop to the same level or slightly below the 1974 level. That is really a disaster because it means, in effect, a halving of farm incomes. It is no wonder that the thoughts and attentions of farmers have been directed toward the need for farm credit. The incomes generated on farms have not been adequate. This particular bill, this move to attempt to free up more funds through the Farm Credit Corporation, will assist; but I hope that the government and the minister will focus more attention on doing something about the real problem, the farm income problem, and will get on with programs for improved marketing and better stabilization which will bring us better net farm incomes.

Mr. Speaker, it is with great pleasure that I now speak to the amendment to the Farm Credit Act. The Canadian Farm Credit Corporation has been in existence for 22 years, during which period it has made about 147,500 loans totalling $5.1 billion. With its long-term credit programs it has been a major force in helping Canadian farmers to increase their production and efficiency during the last 20 years. The corporation has financed more than 60 per cent of long-term farm credit in recent years. The remaining funds were provided by provincial agencies, banks, credit unions and through private loans. Since 1973, the total amount of long-term farm credit has increased at an annual rate of almost 20 per cent, rising from $655 million in 1975 to about $1.9 billion in 1980. This trend is expected to continue, and it will therefore become increasingly important to ensure that the Farm Credit Corporation has an adequate and stable source of funding.
In 1980-81, the last year for which complete statistics are available, the corporation approved 4,686 loans totalling $508 million. A regional breakdown for the year 1980-81 shows that British Columbia received 175 loans totalling $21,597,000. Alberta had 640 loans totalling $71,739,000 and in Saskatchewan farmers received 1,346 loans totalling $128 million.
