speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thought you probably picked the wrong individual to second my motion since the response is to come from the parliamentary secretary.
The motion originates back in July, 1980 when I was sent as a Canadian observer to the sixteenth Caribbean regional conference. However, my interest in the Caribbean goes back many, many years before that. I guess my first interest was when I visited Barbados many years ago after Trans-Canada Airlines had completed the airport on that island, the completion of which airport led to a substantial increase in tourism in Barbados and the resulting improvement in the economy of that island.
I personally was enchanted with Barbados. In fact, I termed it paradise island. I love the people, their attitude, and above all, I like the music. I mention the music because I will be referring to it in connection with another island in a moment.
I want to tell a couple of stories about Barbados which are pertinent. I talked to one of the barmen at the hotel where I was staying. He had been in Florida for some time. I asked him why he was working in Barbados at a much lower salary than he could get in Florida. He said it was simply because of the wonderful life, that there was a lot more in life than just earning a high salary.
I must agree with him because on that very happy island, when you look at the children very seldom do you see a child crying. They were always well dressed, particularly on Sunday. It was a pleasure to see them going to church on Sunday dressed in their finery.
I remember during my first visit there the emphasis on some of the social problems of these islands. As most people are aware, the majority of the inhabitants of Barbados in those days were what might be termed illegitimate. The church had gone to some length to try to get couples together to be married.
I watched a wedding ceremony. Along with the couple being married was a long line of their children. The observation was made to me that this couple was very brave. Because of their religious beliefs, they were getting married. In return, government assistance for their children was being cut off. As long as they were living in sin and their children were illegitimate, government assistance was available to them. When they got married, they had to start supporting their children. That is indicative of some of the problems in the islands of the Caribbean.
I have been very fortunate in the many years since, having been able to visit many of the Caribbean Islands from Bermuda in the north, through Bahamas and Puerto Rico, right through to the south, including the island of Cuba. I refer to Cuba because one cannot help but notice the difference in an island that is run by a dictatorship.
The first observation is that it seems as if one in three of the male population is in uniform. The difference in the music on that island is something that one cannot help noticing immediately inasmuch as it seems to be disciplined. It is almost as if the people who are playing are playing from music, which they
January 28, 1982

cannot do. They have never been taught from music. It is not the same rhythm. I attribute it to the conditions that pertain in that island.
I did observe while I was there that one of the things they are doing in Cuba is trying to provide a good education for the children. I visited the schools. I noticed the children were well dressed and well disciplined. I could not help but think that if that situation continues, in the years ahead the children in Cuba, because of the ease of communication with Florida and the southern states, will probably want to change the nature of the country in which they live.
Another one of my interests in the Caribbean of which 1 have spoken in this House on several occasions deals with the sugar industry. One knows that the giant controlling industry in the sugar business throughout the world is Tate and Lyle. It is installed in several islands including Bermuda, Jamaica, Guyana and Trinidad. I hope to speak in this House on other occasions, as I have done in the past. I am disappointed that the Foreign Investment Review Agency and the government have failed to enforce the regulation made by FIRA that Tate and Lyle divest itself of its interest in Redpath Sugars. Those two or three speeches which I made on this subject in the House are on record.
There are some very special problems in the islands of the Caribbean. The disadvantages of island developing derive from a combination of several characteristics of which the most fundamental and most easily identifiable factor is that of size of population and production. An inadequate reservoir of human resources, of potential producers, consumers or taxpayers to facilitate the attainment of self-generating development mitigate against development and, of course, give rise to serious communication problems.
Many Caribbean countries suffer from a limited and in some cases virtually non-existent natural resource base. Such countries are therefore more vulnerable to the disruptions caused by outside influences. Limited population and available land area inevitably expose a country to a greater extent to adversity, whether a natural disaster such as a hurricane or the incipient effects of brain drain.
Whilst I was in the British Virgin Islands in the month of July, 1980, I talked with a government representative from St. Lucia, Mr. Bruce Williams. He recounted to me how much the Island of St. Lucia is in need of assistance for development purposes. He pointed out that the Island of St. Lucia offers valuable incentives for hotel projects, condominiums, holiday villages and also industries. As he says, they enjoy seven years of tax holiday. He also pointed out, of course, that Canadians like St. Lucia, which is a bilingual country. After reviewing the figures which were supplied to me by the Department of External Affairs as well as representatives of the Canadian International Development Agency prior to my visit to the British Virgin Islands, I noted that our imports from the countries of the Caribbean outdistanced the value of our exports to those same countries by a ratio of approximately 2 to 1. I was studying the Commonwealth Caribbean countries of Barbados, Belize, Guyana, Jamaica, Trinidad, Antigua,
Commonwealth Caribbean
Dominica, Grenada, Montserrat, St. Kitts, St. Lucia and St. Vincent, and in almost all cases we import from these countries approximately $2 of goods for every $1 that we export back to them. This would indicate to me that we need to look at this imbalance and I suggest that could be beneficial to our own Canadian manufacturers.
On my return from the British Virgin Islands, I wrote to the president of the Canadian International Development Agency, Mr. Marcel Masse, and I stated that in my opinion there is no over-all reviewing body which looks at the total picture, including private and institutional activity and the efforts of the other major assisting nations, the United States and Great Britain. Such a co-ordinating or information-gathering body might affect the direction, amount or the form of aid which we have provided. 1 am particularly interested in education in the islands.
While in the British Virgin Islands attending the Commonwealth regional conference, I met a group of Canadian teachers who advised me that their federation was funded in part by CIDA. This item is not shown on any listing of aid for the Carribbean that I had received from CIDA prior to my visit to the Caribbean.
I put a question to Mr. Masse which said:
Of the 17 Commonwealth countries of which I understand seven are dependent, do you have a consistent policy as to which countries you are willing to assist, either directly or indirectly?
Mr. Masse stated in his reply:
In your recent letter, you made reference to the need for an over-all reviewing body which would examine the total picture of aid flows to the Caribbean region. By way of background to your inquiry, I should explain that there was in fact a major interdepartmental review made of the Caribbean region which was spearheaded by the Department of External Affairs. All aspects of Canadian interests were looked into as well as the levels of co-operation of other major donors. This review resulted in a document that is presently being considered by the government. It should assign objectives in a co-ordinated fashion to the various governmental organizations involved in the Caribbean.
A little further down in the letter he continues:
-I can only answer by referring to the interdepartmental review that I have mentioned above.
Thus, on December 8, 1980, while still awaiting the set of documents, I thought that the best step to take was to put a motion on the Order Paper asking for the production of documents of interest to persons looking at the situation in the Caribbean. This I did.
A month later, in January of 1981, I noted a rather interesting article in the Ottawa Citizen by Dian Cohen. She starts off by saying:
Consider these facts about the Caribbean:
300,000 Canadians vacation there each year.
$200 million in Canadian exports are destined for its tropical islands.
$400 million Canadian invested in enterprises there.
$35 million a year is given on our behalf by the Canadian International Development Agency to help West Indians become more affluent in their own countries.

January 28, 1982
Commonwealth Caribbean
Later in the article she goes on:
Could it be possible that our goodwill, our good money, our sophisticated technology and expertise are not being put to proper use? Is it conceivable that a prime reason why the gap between "rich" and "poor" is growing wider rather than narrowing is that our leaders don't know what they're doing?
On March 9, a headline in The Globe and Mail read "Problems still plague Caricom as defenders seek co-operation". On March 21, in The Financial Post there was a headline which stated "Canada can celebrate Antigua independence." It speaks of the Canadian banks in Antigua; the Royal Bank, the Bank of Nova Scotia, the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce, and it speaks of the garment industry which is Canadian, of the condominiums owned by Canadians, a paint factory and several hotels in which there is Canadian equity participation. It goes on to say:
All these are dwarfed, however, by the multimillion dollar public projects, including the construction of a new airport for C$10 million, funded by the Canadian International Development Agency, supervised by an official on loan from the federal Department of Transport in Ottawa-
Then the article continues:
Other CIDA projects are the extension and modernization of Antigua's telephone system, school construction and assistance in irrigation. The Canadian Executive Service Overseas is involved in setting up a new prison and rehabilitation system and the Canadian Caribbean scholarship scheme is involved in vocational training.

Mr. Speaker, since we are on the subject of Canadian aid in the Caribbean, I would like to say a few words about the very substantial contribution being made by CUSO. This body, which started out without any assistance in the way of public funds, now receives a large part of its main budget from the Canadian International Development Agency. In some islands in the Caribbean where Canada has no official representative, CUSO is the only visible Canadian presence. CUSO is a non-governmental organization which co-ordinates the recruitment of Canadians who are prepared to work in Third World countries, including the Caribbean area. CUSO workers include teachers, nurses, agricultural and horticultural experts, technicians, fishery experts and food specialists. Thirty-two CUSO workers are now on assignment in various islands in the Caribbean. This number includes nationals working in various projects administered by CUSO. However, CUSO is not exclusively concerned with the transfer of human resources.
During the past few years, CUSO has become well known for supporting self-development projects. Its programs focus on development and change instead of being a straight transfer of technology and staff. CUSO assignments involve a training aspect, and projects supported by CUSO are expected to involve, and to be initiated by the local population.
CUSO helps to set up local non-governmental organizations that eventually will be able to manage their own affairs without outside help. Especially in the smaller islands in the eastern Caribbean, where almost half of the population is under 25 and three-quarters of the local people are unemployed, CUSO is supporting local co-operative projects specifically designed to create jobs. Two examples are the farm co-operative in Grenada and the craft co-operative in Dominica.
CUSO's involvement in such projects covers every stage, from initial planning up to the production and marketing of the finished product. Aid is given in the form of funding, materials and human resources. Each project has an educational aspect that ensures the continuity of the main goal: self-sufficiency.
Although a large part of CUSO's main budget is funded by CIDA, CUSO also receives valuable contributions from other sources, including Third World governments and agencies that pay the salaries of Canadian experts and provide housing, volunteer workers in Canada who give their time and energy to recruiting and selecting CUSO workers, and finally, educational institutions across Canada that provide office space and help with the agency's administration. Finally, the body receives financial contributions from a number of pharmaceutical companies, radio and television stations and newspapers and periodicals. Thanks to these contributions, CUSO's costs in keeping an expert overseas are much lower than for a number of other agencies, including CIDA. I believe, Mr. Speaker, that there are agencies working in the Caribbean-
It was important for me to have some information from the government as to the way these various groups co-ordinated their activities.
If I have 30 seconds left, I want to refer to the committee report which was tabled in this House on December 8. As a result of reading that report, which was presented by a committee which was formed on March 18, 1981, I came to the conclusion that the information which the Department of External Affairs-I assume it was that department-was unwilling to provide to me was essential for a better understanding of the problems in the Caribbean. Thus, on December 16 of last year I asked that this motion be transferred, after waiting over one year-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to take just a few minutes of the time of the House to speak about this notice of motion for the production of papers, to urge the government to produce the papers requested by our friend from Montreal and perhaps to make a comment or two about that.
I believe we should have more freedom of information in this country. We should not be so nervous about providing information to the public and to Members of Parliament. That is only one part of what we must do to make this place more meaningful.
January 28, 1982

I cannot help but think that Parliament is not really working. As an institution it is not really working as it should for opposition members or for government backbenchers. I think we have to reform the rules of this place to make it much more democratic, to make it a place where Members of Parliament actually become legislators, rather than just rubber stamps for government policy or opposition members whose only power is to make speeches, and try to motivate public opinion so we can change the opinions of the executive or the cabinet. I hope Members of Parliament will speak in this House and lobby for some meaningful change. Of course, members of the government must be included in this effort as well.
If the government were to produce papers when requested and make things public, that would be one small step in a direction that is very important in terms of making this institution meaningful, making it work and making our work here useful and worth while to the Canadians who have elected us to this very honourable institution.
In terms of the issue itself, the hon. member who has just spoken referred to the importance of the Caribbean, and I cannot help but agree with him that it is a very important part of the world to our country. As we look at our own country, we see a country of many, many miles of tremendous resources, of mountains, lakes, streams, great prairies and great forest regions. We have almost everything we need in Canada, with perhaps one gereral exception, and that is a warm, tropical, southern climate. The United States has that. I suppose the southern part of China has that. The southern part of the Soviet Union has that, but that is really all we lack.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
subtopic: EXCHANGES BETWEEN CANADA AND COMMONWEALTH CARIBBEAN
speechtext:
What about Toronto?
Mir. Nystrom: Not even in Toronto do we have that kind of climate. The minister responsible for housing has a lot of hot air from time to time, but we lack that, and it seems to me that the natural place to make up for it is the Caribbean. We are not very far away from the Caribbean countries, and if we had a trading link with Caribbean countries which was more substantial, 1 think that would be something which would be of great benefit to us as Canadians and also of great benefit to the people who live in the many Caribbean countries.
The part of Canada this trading link would help the most would be the Atlantic provinces, Newfoundland and part of Quebec. That is the natural shipping route between Canada and the Caribbean. There are many things we produce in this country that people in the Caribbean could use. We produce many technological products. We have an aerospace industry and a telecommunications industry. There have been advances in relation to railways and aeroplane motors. We have expertise in hydroelectricity, forestry and so forth. We could provide many things to Caribbean countries to help them develop, to help them become more self-sufficient and more advanced, more developed and more prosperous as a society. In return, we could be importing much more from them. We could be importing things we cannot produce in our own country, such as tropical fruits, bananas and commodities of that sort. We
Commonwealth Caribbean
could be importing cotton, sugar and many of the commodities we now import from the United States.
Our trade policy puts too many eggs in one basket, the American basket. About 70 per cent of our trade is with the United States, and it is important that we diversify that trade. Of course, it goes without saying that the United States will remain our main trading partner. We are neighbours. We share a border stretching thousands of kilometres. It is very natural that we trade back and forth. But I think it is also very important that we do not build a store in this country to sell to one customer only, because when we have only one customer, we become totally dependent on the economy of that one customer. If the United States retrenches or becomes more protectionist, that will affect Canadians very drastically.
If we are to diversify our trade, the natural place to look is to an area of the world which, in terms of proximity, is very close to us, and that is the Caribbean, a part of the world which exports products we do not have. It has a tropical climate and exports tropical produce, and it is very close to us. I might also say that it is a part of the world which has two linguistic groups.

Many people in the Caribbean speak French. French is very widely spoken in Martinique, Guadeloupe, Haiti and, as the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert) already mentioned, there are also many places such as St. Lucia where both French and English are spoken. It is very important for Canada as a bilingual country to have trade relations with countries that have a similar cultural badkground.

These are just some of the advantages of trying to escalate and improve our relations with the Caribbean.
Hon. members might remember that at one time a member of my party, Mr. Max Saltsman, then the hon. member for Cambridge, went as far as to suggest one cold winter day in the House of Commons, that we talk to representatives of the Turks and Caicos Islands about the possibility of their becoming a province of Canada. That idea was examined and pursued by officials of both the Turks and Caicos Islands and Canada. Without endorsing the idea or rejecting it, I think that just demonstrated that there is a natural affinity, a natural friendship and a natural pattern which should be pursued and encouraged in the two countries.
In this respect I think of Cuba. During the difficult years in the 1960s under the Diefenbaker government and the Pearson government, Canada continued to have diplomatic and trade relations with Cuba when the United States cut theirs off. I think that was very important. It is very important that we continue our ties with the Cubans in the years which lie ahead.
Before sitting down, I want to make one general comment about trade and why we should diversify our trade and our contacts with the Caribbean and other parts of the world. Up until now, in addition to being dependent on the United States we have also been very dependent on being an exporter of raw materials. I noticed just the other day, for example, that in

January 28, 1982
Commonwealth Caribbean
1980 we had a net surplus in terms of export of raw materials of $23 billion. On the other hand, we had a net deficit in terms of finished products or finished goods of some $18 billion. That is the worst record of any industrialized country in the world, Mr. Speaker.
We all know that resources are very important to us-in my province potash, grain, oil, gas and in Quebec, hydroelectricity and so on. In addition to all that, it is important in terms of jobs to diversify; it is important in terms of jobs to start processing and semi-processing more of our goods before they are exported, and it is important, in terms of jobs, to start doing some things that we can do ourselves and that other countries such as Japan, France, Germany and others in Europe are doing.
I think that in this country we are going to have to put a lot more emphasis on trying to become specialists in more areas such as processing our raw materials and on trying to export more processed goods.
In 1608 when Champlain first opened a trading post in Quebec, it was primarily to have a point at which to gather furs, beaver pelts and so on in order to export them to Europe. Unfortunately, we have not changed our trade policy very much since the days of Champlain. We must make changes if we are to survive in a highly competitive world market.
About 25 per cent of our work force has jobs which are related to the export market. We now have a big problem of unemployment in this country, in large part because trade is becoming more and more competitive. We are moving into the post-industrial age but other nations such as Japan, France and other European countries are moving faster. We will have to start scrambling in order to catch up, never mind moving ahead.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I want to encourage the government to produce the papers requested by my friend from Quebec. I want to encourage the government to make public as soon as possible the plans the government House leader has for reforms of the rules of this institution so that MPs can be legislators and not just chronic bitchers and cryers and rubber stamps for government policy.
I should also like to encourage the government and Canada as a whole to continue expanding and improving our links, and trade with the Caribbean and with trade there. That part of the world can provide something that we do not have-a tropical climate, lots of sunshine and lots of produce from that sunshine. In return, that can help the economy of Atlantic Canada because of the natural shipping pattern that exists. As an industrialized nation with advanced technology, we could give people in that part of the world an extra boost to help develop their economies in the years that lie ahead.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ron Irwin (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXCHANGES BETWEEN CANADA AND COMMONWEALTH CARIBBEAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the hon. member for Vaudreuii (Mr. Herbert) for bringing this
motion before the House. The hon. member is not really complaining about the rules, as was suggested by the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom). He knows the rules very well, and the day we produce all the documents he wants is the day that he will have no opportunity to speak about the things of substance that he cares for! He talked about trade, aid, lack of information in general-and not specifically to him-about the Caribbean. He spoke about tourism, about sugar-he has spoken about sugar at least half a dozen times, and I thank him for that. The hon. member for Yorkton-Melville has a valid point about all our eggs being in one basket. In 1980, we did a total export business of $73.8 billion and a total import business of $68.7 billion. Of this, $46 billion of export was with the United States and $48 billion was import business with the United States. Approximately $90 billion business was done with the United States last year. If there is a criticism of Canadians in general and not just governments, it is that we must treat the Caribbean and South America much more seriously than we have to date.
I should like, first of all, to look at the broad problem of what is happening in the world. The foremost problem is poverty, and this is shown by what is happening in the Caribbean and South America. The poorest country is Haiti where the gross national product per capita is $260 per year. The 2.5 billion of the world's poorest people depend for almost all their energy needs upon wood and agricultural residues. Of the world's 150 countries, 100 consume more food than they produce. At the present rate, the world's forest cover will be halved by the year 2000 because we are cutting the forests down for fuel and energy-things that they should not be used for-because better sources of energy have not been developed in these various nations.
By the year 2000 there will be two billion more people on this planet. We spent almost a year on the Constitution and perhaps we are inclined to forget the reality of the rest of the world until we see that each year 15 million children under the age of five die, mostly from water-borne diseases. Next year 15 million children will die for the same reasons. Three quarters of the world's population consumes 15 per cent of its commercial energy, and 90 million people in the world are short of firewood.
The parliamentary task force on North-South relations recently issued a report in which it dealt with the 800 million people who live in conditions of absolute poverty. The criteria of absolute poverty are unbelievable. It means that only four out of ten children complete more than three years of primary school. Of every ten children born, two die within a year, another dies before age five and only five survive to age 40. A child that contracts measles has a 200 per cent more chance of death than a Canadian child.
The task force report has the following to say:
Half of those people live in south Asia, mainly in India and Bangladesh. A sixth live in east and southeast Asia, mainly in Indonesia. Another sixth are in sub-Saharan Africa. The rest-about 100 million people-are divided among Latin America, North America and the Middle East.
January 28, 1982

It is ironic that in the second paragraph on the same page the report states "some $500 billion is spent each year for military purposes." Yet so little is spent on important things such as shelter, food, and economic stability.
Why should our policy regarding the Caribbean be different from that of the United States? Sometimes I think that the United States has had so much trouble in the last number of years when it has been picking losers, that we should let them choose first and then pick the other side!
Our major contribution in the Caribbean so far has been tourism. Maybe that is why there are so many experts on the Caribbean in Canada who know so little about it.
For certain valid reasons we are moving out of the Caribbean. For instance, we are going to Australia for aluminium. The main reason, however, is that this country had had two decades of easy times in trading with other countries. What has happened in the last ten years is that there has been an increase in exports with Third World countries from $1.7 billion to $8.8 billion, while with the Commonwealth Caribbean the increase has been from $123 million to $286 million. In other words, the increase has been fivefold and sixfold with Third World countries but only double with the Commonwealth Caribbean.
In our travels through Caribbean countries we were told repeatedly that we were not competitive. We were told that our businesses were shifting to the more affluent industrialized areas such as Brazil, Venezuela, Mexico and perhaps Argentina and Chile, and that in areas where it is difficult to operate, Canadian businessmen have folded their tents. Prior to what was done this year, it was almost embarrassing that Trinidadian aid in 1980 to the Caribbean was greater than that of Canada-aid from a little country like that!
I think what was said by the hon. member for Vaudreuil was absolutely accurate. The fault is that we require more information. We may have to bring in trading companies and credit mix. We may have to provide more money and more facilities for Canadian businessmen dealing in that particular area. We may need more face-to-face discussion with government officials. We need much more education on what is happening in the southern half of this great area.
Let us look at the United States policy. The United States has had almost a disastrous two decades of supporting governments which have fallen. In the process there have been some atrocious governments. In 1953 or 1954, I was in Cuba and saw the combination of Batista organized crime and United States interests in Cuba. It was wrong then for the United States to support that regime. Canada was wise in not getting involved in that decade of hate which evolved around Cuba. Canada was wise to keep its dialogue open with the present administration. In 1979, the United States received at least half a dozen jolts. In Nicaragua the Somoza regime was replaced by the Sandinistra regime. In Grenada, Eric Gairy was replaced by the new JEWEL movement. In Surinam there was a semi-leftist coup. On top of this, Iran erupted and
Commonwealth Caribbean
finally, just recently, there was the assassination of President Sadat in Egypt. The Rear Admiral and Naval Commander of the Caribbean, Robert P. Mackenzies, said that Nicaragua, Grenada and Cuba were "practically one country". Consequently the United States policy is different from ours. It is to provide direct aid to a specific country which fosters direct United States interest, usually business. This is why Canadians are so well accepted in the Caribbean-we have no colonial aspirations; we do not support governments for philosophical reasons resulting in profit; we support governments in the Caribbean because we think it is right. This is why we are ad idem with Venezuela.
At the present time Venezuela is the only major democratic option to Marxism and communism in the Caribbean. Prior to Venezuela becoming interested in the Caribbean and starting to expand, what did poor people do? They either lived in poverty and their children and grandchildren lived in poverty, or they resorted to guerrilla tactics and civil war. There was no other option except Cuban exploitation. They either lived in poverty and stayed there, or they aligned themselves with Cuban export of guerrilla warfare until Venezuela started to export not only philosophy but a few dollars, along with Trinidad and Mexico.
Last year the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacGuigan) reported to the CARICOM ministers in Jamaica that we would give the Commonwealth Caribbean priority status. After the conference he indicated that there were certain countries which would be targeted by Canada. He specifically named countries such as Venezuela. In the interim we have done everything to try to build a connection between Canada and Venezuela. I do not think we should kid ourselves; because we talk of the Caribbean here and talk of our importance there, we are not that important yet. We should be, but we will not be unless we make the effort. Also the minister announced a framework. The major elements of the framework announced at the CARICOM conference were as follows:
All countries in the Commonwealth Caribbean, regardless of level of development, will be eligible for Canadian development assistance, with special attention on the LDCs of the eastern Caribbean.
LDCs refers to least developed countries. They continue:
Canadian development assistance will focus on the promotion of sustained economic growth and development.
With self-reliance of the recipient countries, the ultimate objective:
(a)	Canada will increase its ODA levels in real terms;
(b)	increased levels of technical assistance will be provided for economic and financial management in the public sector and for improving private sector management and productivity;
(c)	increased support for industrial co-operation will be given;
(d)	at the regional level, Canada will focus on supporting the Caribbean Development Bank, on essential common services, where appropriate, and on regional institution building and co-operation including that with CARICOM.
What does this mean? In dollars and cents it has some meaning. For the fiscal year 1981-82, we will almost double our assistance to the Caribbean to $55.3 million. This will be in addition to the $6 million already announced for Jamaica in support of its economic recovery program. Funds will be used

January 28, 1982
Commonwealth Caribbean
for specific countries as follows: Barbados, up to $2.6 million; Belize, up to $1.5 million; Dominican Republic, up to $2.3 million; Guyana, up to $7.5 million; Haiti, up to $7.2 million; Jamaica, up to $10 million; Leeward and Windward Islands, up to $11 million. The funds to the Caribbean Development Bank will be up to $4.3 million. Industrial co-operation will be up to $2.5 million. Non-governmental organizations will be up to $4.5 million. Our total aid to the Commonwealth Caribbean will be $43 million, which is more than double what it was last year.
We will also be providing bilateral assistance as follows: up to $30 million for Guyana, up to $41 million for Jamaica, up to $44 million for the Leeward and Windward Islands, and up to $25 million for Barbados and Belize. Also Canada will provide non-bilateral assistance to the tune of $85 million which will be administered through the Caribbean Development Bank.
It is important to treat each one of these sectors as individual sectors. There is a misconception among Canadians that Caribbean people know each other well. The truth is that they do not. Many of these countries are large islands and are more familiar with the United States than they are with their neighbours. We must develop a separate policy to fit in with the culture and the economy of each individual area. Within the remaining time I will try to run through some of these countries. I will start with El Salvador. Right now the option which the president and the people of El Salvador have is either to try to become democratic with the aid of countries such as Venezuela, or to succumb to another revolution. I find it rather humorous that we in the House try to impose our democratic standards on a country that has not really had an election in over 50 years and in which there is civil insurrection. I think some of the members who are really attacking the electoral process that is evolving in El Salvador are more interested in getting headlines in Ontario than they are in the welfare of that particular country. They do not really understand. There is only one man there standing between the country and another dictatorship, whether it be a communist one or the normal type of dictatorship which the people have known in these regions of the Caribbean and South America, and that man is President Duarte. President Duarte has been a democrat for over 20 years. He was a mayor and he was a member of the opposition. He is president of El Salvador. On his right side he has the army and the rich and on the left side he has the poor and the guerrillas. In this House we repeatedly attack the government of El Salvador, which is really President Duarte. We do not attack the right or the left. We attack the only man who has a chance of bringing a democratic process into El Salvador.
I do not know one member of this House who deplores the fact that 26,000 people have been killed in that country or who deplores the instability in El Salvador. I think we should, as former prime minister Lester B. Pearson once said, bury our differences at our waterline when it comes to our foreign policy. We are not doing that. Consequently, by attacking
what President Duarte is doing, we are not really espousing human rights there or in any other place in the world.
Venezuela is probably our most important partner in the southern hemisphere economically. We exported to them $641 million worth of goods last year, but we imported from Venezuela over $2 billion worth of goods. I think our Canadian businessmen should be much more aware of that imbalance. They should be prepared to go to Venezuela to sell our goods with the help of the Canadian government. Venezuela needs wheat. Is it not odd that a country we traditionally think of as being rich in agriculture cannot support itself for such reasons as that it has no water or that the weather is too hot? This also applies to the Bahamas. Venezuela needs pigs. We sell pigs, but we do not sell pigs to Venezuela. Venezuela needs certain technology, but we are not selling that to them. Meanwhile we buy $2 billion worth of goods from Venezuela, an ally with whom we agree philosophically. I think the parliamentary task force report dealing with trade is completely accurate. This report of the Special Committee on a National Trading Corporation, issued June, 1981, stated:
Canada has only a minimal position in many of-

Mr. Speaker, it appears that I have only four minutes in which to speak, the last speaker having gone one minute over his time. I want to deal with the motion. I cannot understand why the parliamentary secretary did not deal with the motion instead of telling us all the things he did. The motion is simple. It asks for the production of papers and communications during the last year between the government and the communities of the Commonwealth Caribbean relating to the exchange of commodities and technology, the exchange of students, tariff changes and other measures to improve trade, tourism and cultural exchanges. But the parliamentary secretary did not say one word about any of that. Why is the government refusing to give us this type of information? Surely to goodness Canadians, particularly members of the House, are entitled to this kind of information.
The parliamentary secretary tells us that we will continue to give to the Caribbean area $55 million, $6 million, $43 million and $85 million. He did not say one word about what we are getting for this money. He did not tell us what is being produced. He did not say anything about the extravagance or waste. He did not say anything about the low interest we are charging or indeed if this money is being given away while Canadians have to pay high interest rates. Why is the government not giving us this information? Is the government afraid to do so? Is it because the government is being extravagant? Is it because the government is giving this money and nothing is resulting?
The members on the other side of the House are saying that they live in absolute poverty, yet they live in a climate where

production could be high. Why does Canada not make sure when making contributions to these countries that the money is used to increase production and not used as welfare purposes? That is what Canada should be doing. Why are we granting low-interest rates to these countries and yet charging high interest rates to Canadians? Even our own Indian band councils cannot get money at these low rates. Why does the government not answer questions? Is the government afraid? The government is refusing to give us the information and, therefore, people have to reach their own conclusions. Some of the information I have seen in information sheets from the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacGuigan) and from CIDA indicate that in many cases the money is being wasted. What about Grenada? Two hundred thousand dollars was spent for a garage in Grenada. What are we doing? We are helping a military build-up so that the communists can step in and get along a lot better. I am not in favour of helping communists in any country. I am in favour of helping people to help themselves. We should not give money away at low interest rates while charging high rates to Canadians. What about these amounts of $55 million, $6 million, $43 million and $85 million? The parliamentary secretary brags about this. But I want to know what the government is doing with this money. What good is it doing? Are we simply handing this money out as a gift from the people of Canada? Why does the government not answer the questions? What is the government afraid of? That is what I would like to know. That is what the people of Canada would like to know.
I am not going to talk this bill out. I am going to give hon. members over there a chance to vote in favour of this bill. If they had any guts, they would force the government to provide this kind of information.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to resume my comments on the amendment to the Farm Credit Act as I was then explaining that during 1980-81, which is the last year for which full statistics are available, the Corporation approved 4,686 loans amounting to $508.8 million. For example, British Columbia, Mr. Speaker, obtained 175 loans amounting to $21,597,000. Alberta 640 for a total of $71,739,000. Saskatchewan, 1.346 for $128,456,000. Manitoba, 470 for $47,052,000. Ontario, 1,084 for $138,308,000. Quebec, 742 for $80,961,000 and the Atlantic provinces, 229 lor $20,769,000.
Mr. Speaker, the Farm Credit Corporation also has outstanding loans under the Farm Credit Act of March 31, 1980. In this regard, British Columbia accounts for $111,440,000, Alberta for $594,533,000, Saskatchewan for $876,686, Manitoba for $306,275,000, Ontario for $917,487,000, Quebec for $413,587,000 and the Atlantic region for $81 million. Mr. Speaker, the purpose of the Farm Credit Corporation is to help as many young farmers as possible, and in fact, the majority of approved loans are granted to people under 35. Their share has remained relatively constant at 70 per cent in the last three years. Indeed, 3 per cent of all approved loans were granted under the special loans program for new farmers under which the borrowers can keep an outside full-time job for up to five years while they get their farm operation under way.
As for the purpose of the loans, about 27.9 per cent of those approved last year were used to purchase additional land compared with 29.8 per cent the previous year. Other loans can be classified as follows: new units, 24.4 per cent; permanent improvements, 16.5 per cent; mortgages, 12.3 per cent; other debts, 12 per cent; equipment, 2.3 per cent; livestock, 2.2 per cent and miscellaneous, 2.4 per cent.
The repayment record of farmers has remained favourable in 1980-81. Of the $75.2 million due during the period, 89.4 per cent has been repaid and the farmers have also repaid $52.2 million on the undue principal. During the year, 91.9 per cent of the $279.1 million in due interest was paid. At the end of the last fiscal year, 93 per cent of the active accounts of the

January 28, 1982
Farm Loans
Farm Credit Corporation were in order compared with 93.2 per cent the previous year. Real losses on these loans amounted to $1,537,000, or 1.4 per cent of the portfolio of the FCC.
During the current fiscal year, from April 1, 1981, to January 15, 1982, the Farm Credit Corporation approved 4,328 loans for a total of nearly $429 million. According to the estimates, the total budget for this year will reach nearly $455 million. We can only give approximate figures since an important part of the total budget of the corporation is made up of reimbursements or advanced payments by the borrowers.
Up to this point for this year, the major purpose of the loans seems to be the purchase of additional land, closely followed by the purchase of new units. Flowever, the number of loans for debt consolidation purposes has increased markedly because of the crisis triggered by high interest rates which reached 24.8 per cent on March 31, 1980, and 27.1 per cent on September 30, 1981.
The FCC is quite aware of the fact that the profit-earning capacity of credit is directly related to a borrower's managing ability, and that tight management of a farm has never been more important than over the past few years, because of the instability of interest rates. That is why it also provides a counselling service on a voluntary basis to all borrowers, old and new, who apply for it. The purpose of this service is to give advice in the areas of organization, planning and management, and thus help families living on farms to achieve their economic and individual objectives. As of December 1, 1981, some 3,025 borrowers were availing themselves of this service.
The corporation also administers the Farm Syndicates Credit Act which makes loans to farmers who are willing to join forces to beat the high costs associated with the individual purchase and use of machinery, equipment and buildings. Loans are made available to syndicates of three or more farmers up to $100,000 or $15,000 per individual farmer, whichever is the smaller. In 1980-81, the FCC lent $4.8 million to syndicates, representing 169 loans. Between April, 1981, and January, 1982, it lent them $5.4 million, representing 171 loans. Therefore, there has been clearly a marked increase in the demand for this type of loan over the past few years, and it is due especially to the rising cost of sophisticated farm implements.
In this respect, I cannot help but think about my own riding and the way this new amendment should help the farmers of the Beauce region who are so close to me. Being a farmer myself, I am one of them. I am proud of my constituency which accounts for 40 per cent of all the maple syrup produced in North America. I am sure that with this new amendment and the new Crown corporation Canagrex, we shall be able to export the maple syrup of Beauce. That will be of interest not only to Beauce but also to neighbouring ridings, such as those of Levis, Bellechasse, Montmagny, Megantic-Compton-Stanstead and Frontenac which are not far from mine. To my mind, it will be a very good thing for all those farmers and maple syrup producers, Mr. Speaker.
Last week, I had the pleasure of welcoming to my office a great friend of mine, Mr. Victor Poirier, chairman of the board of maple syrup producers of Beauce. He told me that there still remains to be sold on the market in Beauce some 468,000 pounds of maple syrup. They are still on tap, as we say in Beauce. Well, with the new amendment and the new Crown corporation to be known as Canagrex, I feel sure that our producers in Beauce will be happy to learn that the Canadian government has decided to establish the Crown corporation of Canagrex and that in the future we can sell our syrup outside Quebec and Canada. Then, we of the Liberal party, will be able to tell the people in Beauce, in Quebec and across Canada that the Crown corporation Canagrex is a wonderful thing not only for our own farmers and maple syrup producers in Quebec, but for all farmers throughout Canada.
It is all very well to discuss all that, but something else must be kept in mind: from time to time we also have bankruptcies, and I would like to say a few words about that tonight. I am increasingly concerned as well as the farming community about the fact that from 1979 to 1980, the number of farm bankruptcies has increased from 124 to 222. There have been 261 in 1981, a 17.6 per cent increase over last year. As I said, I hope Canagrex and the amendment will bring about significant improvements. In 1979-80, 32 FCC borrowers went bankrupt compared to 56 in 1980-81. As of January 1, 1982, 70 FCC borrowers had already gone bankrupt. The government certainly recognizes the seriousness of this situation, knowing full well that official bankruptcies are only part of total farm failures.
1 have already suggested that the Farm Credit Corporation should help farmers in distress through counselling assistance. The government itself provided further assistance to those farmers by setting up a special financial assistance program for farmers last November. This $50 million program enables the corporation to make loans to farmers unable to get a Small Business Development Bond from chartered banks. The corporation charges its current 16% per cent interest rate, on those loans, but it also grants a yearly interest rebate equivalent to 5 per cent up to two years. In some cases, the FCC loan must be combined with the Small Business Development Bond, the SBDB, because the farmer needs large sums of money to recapitalize his debts. In such cases, the corporation co-operates with the private sector in the best interests of farmers. In so doing, the government shows its concern for the precarious position of some farmers and its willingness to take concrete steps to help them. Since the program was set up November 12, 1981, the Farm Credit Corporation has approved 89 loans, for a total $11 million, as of January 15, 1982. It is expected that the funds earmarked for the program will be all spent by March 31, 1982.
January 28, 1982

This legislation is a further step toward improving the financial situation of Canadian farmers. The important amendment to the Farm Credit Act that will grant the corporation authority to tap the financial market for funds will enable it to meet the credit needs of farmers adequately.

It is my firm belief that this type of loan must continue to be offered to those Canadian farmers who need it to remain viable. Access to the financial markets may mean that the Farm Credit Corporation will also be able to offer mortgages with interest fixed for shorter terms such as ten years.
The Farm Credit Corporation also plays a vital role in ensuring that all Canadians have access to the advantages offered by a national program. Regional differences can make it more or less attractive for commercial lending institutions to extend credit in a given area. Higher returns can often be obtained by placing their funds in other areas or economic sectors.
The Farm Credit Corporation brings a strong national influence in the field of credit. In areas without provincial credit programs the FCC is almost the only source of financing for young people who want to start farming.
When an organization is established with a clear and distinct mandate, its mission is clear. The Farm Credit Corporation exists for the primary purpose of providing long-term farm credit and advisory services in order to develop viable farm operations. Its programs are therefore sensitive to the needs of farmers and to agriculture. Repayment schedules are tailored to meet the income-generating cycles of production.
In times of serious difficulties in a particular industry a borrower can make arrangements to defer his payments up to two years.
The FCC's philosophy in the administration of its loans is flexibility and service to the farmer. Credit advisers spent hours working on solutions to repayment problems^ and the corporation fosters a lenient collection policy. In making over 70 per cent of its loans to young farmers, the FCC also accepts considerable risks.
Because commercial lending institutions deal primarily with farmers who have an established track record and are regarded as commercially acceptable credit risks, young people-in this case those under 35 years of age-beginning farmers and small farmers are excluded from commercial sources of longterm farm credit. Their exclusion has important policy implications, as it is these farmers who will play an important role in the future of agricultural development and the attainment of the potential envisaged by the agri-food strategy for Canada. Because agricultural production is based almost entirely on the family farm structure, entrants into the sector must be encouraged if the agricultural sector is to maintain or improve productivity levels.
Because of the additional risks in agricultural production, a higher equity ratio is normally required to survive than for other types of businesses. In addition, farmers, like other small businesses, do not have access to debt or equity markets which are available to large businesses. Beginning and small farmers are at an even greater disadvantage than established farmers because they have much less equity and are considered to be too great a risk by commercial lending institutions. Recogniz-
Farm Loans
ing these factors, the risks faced by farmers and the unique credit needs of agriculture in general, most developed countries in the world have specialized agricultural credit programs with preferred terms and preferred conditions.
The Farm Credit Corporation is the government's way of showing its confidence in an industry which, over the years, has proved time and time again that it can, and will, pay its own way. Statistics on arrears and defaults are proof of this.
The FCC also plays a significant role in the transfer of family farms. Without sufficient long-term government credit, the intergenerational transfer of farms will be jeopardized. Out of the total Canadian labour force, those readily available to work in that sector or those wanting to become primary agricultural producers are generally those who have practical farming knowledge and experience. These are usually the sons and daughters of farmers. Without a mechanism by which they can take over the family farm, which is the unit on which Canadian agricultural production is based, human resources required for agricultural production could diminish, resulting in the possibility of decreased productivity of the agricultural sector.
One of the strengths of an organization like the Farm Credit Corporation is the calibre of its staff. I would like to pay a compliment to them. FFC personnel are trained in agriculture and farm management practices. The great majority are sons and daughters of farmers. They are familiar with the needs of the industry and have been trained in advisory services to help the individual applicant.
In 1980-81, 204 credit advisers, these are the front line staff, conducted more than 57,000 interviews in the selection of loan applicants or the administration of loan accounts. The Farm Credit Corporation was only able to approve 17 per cent of the applications received. This represented over half a billion dollars in loan funds, which is a considerable sum. But it is my firm belief that the amendments tabled by the Minister of Agriculture will bring much needed support to the Farm Credit Corporation in its mandate to provide even more assi-tance to Canadian farmers.
The increase in the amount of money that will be made available at a lower rate of interest will go a long way to help promote this.
We all know, Mr. Speaker, that if the farm community is healthy financially, that means that the implement dealer is healthy, the local car dealer is healthy, and the local stores are healthy, and so on down the line.
In conclusion I should like to say that we can never cease to bring forth constructive and useful legislation which will encourage and help farmers to use the initiative that they have demonstrated over the years to build a healthy agricultural community. We must ensure that they will receive a fair return for their products and a fair return on their investment, which is very substantial.

14442

January 28, 1982
Farm Loans
Mir. Gordon Taylor (Bow River): Mr. Speaker, 1 am delighted to have an opportunity to speak on this bill and on agriculture generally, because agriculture generally revolves around credit and income.
I should start off by saying that this bill is certainly no panacea for farmers in this country. It is a step forward but it does not touch the real problems of agriculture in Canada. The real problem, of course, is that farmers do not receive an adequate net income compared to the expenses that they incur.
For a number of years, farm income has remained somewhat stable but the cost of machinery, the cost of transportation, the cost of labour, the cost of everything that the farmer buys has gone up. There has been a constant wearing away of income to the point that it is not now adequate. In the last year, hundreds of farmers who might have been called reasonably well off found themselves in a very bad cash flow position. They may have assets but they do not have the cash to meet everyday expenses. This is a serious problem. Those who have not been farming for a long time have been in a serious position in that they did not have the cash flow and so were not able to get credit.
I want to deal with some items in the bill but I do regard it as a step forward. I will deal with the principle of a number of items. I am happy that the definition of agriculture has been broadened because I think it was too restrictive previously.
1 should like to pay tribute to the officers of the Farm Credit Corporation in Alberta. I do not know the officers in other provinces but Mr. McEwen in Calgary and Mr. Jones in Edmonton carry out an excellent public relations program. They talk to anyone who wants to talk to them about these things and they explain whether they can or cannot meet the application of a farmer. I believe that the farmers of Alberta appreciate that.
Such officers should not be confined to a definition of farming because they know, better than anyone else in the country, what farming is in that province. The former definition held that farming included livestock raising, beekeeping, dairying, fruit growing and all tillage of the soil. That was a fairly wide definition but certain items were not included. I prefer the new definition which incudes livestock raising, beekeeping, dairying, fruit growing, tillage of the soil and any other husbandry activities that the corporation describes in writing as farming. That gives some discretion and some responsibility to the officers of the Farm Credit Corporation. I like that particular clause of the bill.
I am not sure whether I like the next clause. I should have liked to hear the minister say why the board membership has been increased from five members to seven. Today there is a tendency to increase everything, particularly boards. More members on the board means more overhead, more costs, more bureaucracy, and perhaps more Liberals. I hope that for once the government will appoint people because of their ability and not their political stripe.
Maybe the work load of the board is greater than it was when five members were sufficient. I suppose the greater
number gives a little better chance of having a quorum in case some members are absent. If the minister can give us sound reasons for the increase, I am sure the committee will endorse it but if not, I think it should be brought back to five members. After all, Mr. Speaker, the corporation does not do very much of the work. It does the planning and makes the policies, which are now included in the act anyway, but the advisory board, which consists of people in the field, really knows the score and it has most to do with administering of the bill.
The next item that I am interested in is the increase from $150 million to $225 million which is to be paid out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund. Some other members have already spoken about this item. I think the increase is long overdue and I do not think it is enough-perhaps it would be impossible to have enough money to meet the demand. I hope the figure was reached after a survey of the needs of agriculture in the various provinces. That should be the criterion in determining the amount of money to be made available.
No industry in Canada is more important than agriculture, Mr. Speaker. It produces the food of this nation. The family farm has been a major factor in the production of our food, and if we do not make sure that production continues, then in future we may expect to run into severe difficulty.
A few weeks ago we discussed the sterilization or killing of land by pesticides. That is only one item but today there are many others that are taking good agricultural land out of production. That is something that should concern every thinking Canadian. At times there is no other alternative but in many cases there are alternatives. Poor or non-productive land should be used for purposes other than good agricultural land. I hope this $225 million figure was arrived at after careful study of market demands, because it is a very important item.
Then the next clause of the bill deals with Section 13, which is really the key to the entire bill. It is an amendment which will give the corporation additional authority to borrow money. Clause 8(2) reads in part:
At the request of the corporation, the Minister of Finance may, out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund, lend money to the corporation-
As well, Clause 8(1) reads:
The corporation may, with the approval of the Minister of Finance, borrow money by any means, including issuing and selling bonds, debentures, notes and other evidences of indebtedness of the corporation.
I hope "by any means" will mean that they will not suddenly go into the bond market. Over a period of time the Farm Credit Corporation should build up its credibility in regard to this particular item. It should build up its credibility in regard to borrowing. If it does not build up credibility first, it will not receive the best results in borrowing.
In the United States, its corporation may borrow money from pension funds and from various other funds. I hope it is not the purpose of the federation to go to banks to borrow from them. After all, the present rate of interest is 15.75 plus one, which is 16.75 per cent. I would hate to see the Farm Credit Corporation having two interest rates-one with the

money which comes from government revenue, taxpayers money, and one which it must levy to meet the charges for the money it borrows. This would be dynamite and counterproductive; I would hate to see it happen. Some very careful thought must be given to the borrowing of money if we are to keep the common interest rate down. In my view it is too high now. This is not a gift to farmers, it is a loan. Farmers pay interest on it and the Farm Credit Corporation pays the interest to the government. It is earning money for the people of Canada; farmers will pay that money to the people of Canada, for the use of money which belongs to the people of Canada. I do not think it is unsound. It is fair and sensible. But the amount they will pay for the borrowing of that money will have a very important effect.
Perhaps in Alberta the Farm Credit Corporation will be able to borrow from the Alberta Heritage Trust Fund. I understand that it will have the guarantee of the Government of Canada. If so, I do not think there would be any objection from the people of Alberta if this money was lent to the FCC for the use of young farmers in the province. I have not discussed this matter with the trustees of the Alberta Heritage Trust Fund, but I know the trustees well. They are interested in lending money where it will do the most good, where it will help to not only develop farms but the agricultural industry, and will have the effect of increasing employment all the way down the line. There is a possibility that the FCC would be able to borrow money from the fund. After all, the Alberta Agricultural Development Corporation now borrows from the fund and pays a reasonable rate of interest. Because it is receiving a reasonable interest, it is able to give farmers of Alberta a much better deal; probably one of the best deals available any place in Canada. Farmers pay 12 per cent on their borrowings which might have been high a few years ago, but it is quite low when one considers today's rates. Every percentage point means a substantial amount of money out of the pockets of farmers. It also charges 15 per cent to processors. Both those rates are below the interest rates of the FCC. Consequently, there has been a tendency in Alberta to move, wherever possible, to the Agricultural Development Corporation and away from the FCC, although the legislation indicates that ADC is the final borrowing, not the first. The FCC has been out of money; it has not had any money, so it has not been able to accept many applications. The banks will not touch these applications at all, except at prohibitive interest rates. I am not sure whether the policy is still in effect, but at one time the ADC lent money to young beginning farmers at 6 per cent because the objective of the government of Alberta was to keep people on the land, to encourage them to stay there, and to increase production. The entire country benefits when farmers produce.
After building up a good credit rating, it may well be that the Farm Credit Corporation will go on the bond market and do well. I think this is a step forward, giving the FCC the right to borrow money. I hope the section which includes "with the approval of the Minister of Finance" will not be detrimental. I hope the minister views this from a broad horizon because the
Farm Loans
money will be used to develop the country probably as much as any other money in the entire economy.
This section dealing with borrowing is fine, but I wish the minister had gone one step further. I read an article about some easterner who studied farms in Canada. He said that farmers in Alberta were better off than farmers anywhere else in the country. Perhaps that is so for some farmers, but there are farmers in every province, including Alberta, who are having difficult times because of inadequate net incomes. We must recognize this. But there are some farmers who have done well, who have had lucky breaks, who have made the correct decisions and have been able to accumulate considerable wealth. There is no better way to provide an incentive for those farmers who are wealthy, those farmers who have made their money from the land and from agriculture, to invest their money in helping other young people to become farmers and help in the development of the agricultural industry throughout the country. The minister should have provided an incentive in the bill for people who have become wealthy through their farming operations, their ability and their hard work, perhaps some good luck, co-operative weather and making correct lending decisions. Farming is probably one of the biggest gambles in the world. Sometimes a gamble pays off, sometimes it does not. For those with considerable wealth, what would be a better way than supplying them with some incentive to provide money to the FCC; then it could be lent to young farmers to start farming. There is plenty of land available in Alberta. We need more food; the world is hungry for food. We must get our young people on the farms. When one looks at the price of land, of machinery and of getting started today, it is practically prohibitive for any young farmer unless he has extra currency from some place. His father may be able to help him to some degree, but many times it is not sufficient for him to start producing. In fact, the farmer may have several other sons who require some of the wealth he has accumulated. I ask the minister to consider putting incentive into the bill.
If a farmer invests in FCC, it is somewhat like having an RRSP. The farmer will get some benefit from income tax, incentive enough to encourage him to lend his money so that he will put it there instead of putting it in short-term loans. Therefore, it would have to be somewhat comparable. I think this would be excellent. Many people in this country have made good money off the land. They are now looking for places to invest. They would invest in this sort of thing if the government were to provide an incentive and guarantee that three or four years down the road that incentive will not be removed, as has been done with the IAACs and the RRSPs.
That is what takes the breath of life out of our farmers and our people when they see something like that going on. The government has done more harm to itself in this budget than any other single thing by the action it has taken affecting retiring farmers. However, I will deal with that in a few moments. But the government has broken the hearts of many farmers who plan to retire. After all, the land is the farmers'

January 28, 1982
Farm Loans
pension. A farmer has no pension scheme from a government or from a large corporation. Elis only pension scheme is his land. You take that away from him, and you leave him destitute in his old age, destitute in his retirement years. That is a very important item.
Let us deal with one other item. I know we are not in the Committee of the Whole so 1 will not go clause by clause. Nevertheless, I do want to deal with the final section of the bill, an act respecting rebates of interest on farm loans made under the Farm Credit Act. This is an important item. This is the legislation under which the government is making $45 million available plus $5 million for the interest subsidy to help farmers who are in dire straits. It seems as though every time our Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) mentions farmers, he also mentions the words dire straits. I do not know why he does this. Surely our farmers who are on the verge of bankruptcy should be able to seek some help to prevent them getting into dire straits which causes them to lose their farms.
But what does the Canadian Federation of Agriculture say about this bill? I say the minister is telling us that it is doing us some good. I think it will. But the government is providing $45 million for an industry across Canada when probably $500 million would be more appropriate. What does the Canadian Federation of Agriculture say with regard to this particular item? I shall quote for hon. members' benefit as follows:
The FCC refinancing capability of $45 million at 5 per cent under regular FCC rates would be a help if there is a decent amount of funds available to lend. But the $45 million is wholly inadequate. To qualify, you have to be in such bad shape that you can't even get an SBDB loan, and are sure therefore to go under, if you don't get relief. Also, you only get two years of interest relief. The $45 million will in any case only refinance 450 farmers at $100,000 each-
The next paragraph reads:
The FCC provision is a disgracefully inadequate sop to the requests of farmers for some real help. Under the absurd and deceiving budgetary convention that federal investment is called an expenditure, the government says it will spend $50 million to help farmers in trouble.
It is doing nothing of the kind. It is spending $5 million over two years (2.5 per year ) in reducing interest rates. The other $45 million is an interest-bearing loan to farmers that must be repaid. Where a billion dollars of such money is needed, $45 million is provided.
That is what the Federation of Agriculture, which is made up of agricultural people, thinks about this particular bill. I hope it will be able to help some farmers, however. But even if it cannot help everyone, it will help some. I think the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) should take the thoughts of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture to heart and deal with them.
The next item that follows is a very important item also. It involves financing. It involves whether or not farmers will be going to the FCC. The difficulty with the present government, particularly in the field of agriculture as well as almost everything else, is that it does the turkey dance. The government takes one step forward; turkeys only take two steps backwards. The government outwits the turkeys. The government takes one step forward and five or six steps backwards. You cannot advance doing that. It is somewhat akin to what the army does. I had a commanding officer who told us our battalion would never retreat. He said "If things get too bad, I
will say 'about turn, forward march. But we will never retreat'." That is what agriculture is doing. Here we have something that is hurting the farmers and something unnecessary, in my opinion. I am referring to the capital cost allowances. Capital cost allowances are important to farming. A farmer has to buy machinery. Machinery wears out. For many years it was understood that machinery would wear out and that the farmers would be able to write that off in capital cost allowances. On page 41 of the document entitled "The Budget in More Detail", tabled with the budget papers, we read the following under the heading of Capital Cost Allowances:
-it is generally recognized that assets can be written off for tax purposes at much faster rates than is warranted by their actual economic lives.
The income tax people made it very clear that they are recognizing capital cost depreciation. If we take a look at the 1981 farmers' income tax guide, we find that this particular item is dealt with. In order that everyone who is not acquainted with this document will know, I will read what is found on page 9 as follows:
It is, however, recognized that over a number of years these assets wear out or become obsolete.
The government arranges for the person to depreciate this equipment over a period of years. But suddenly the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) thinks that depreciation is too fast, faster than is warranted by their actual economic lives. In other words, a person can depreciate a machine before it is actually worn out and make money from it. On page 2 in "The Budget in More Detail", we read:
In many cases, the capital cost allowance rates are deliberately set in excess of economic depreciation rates in order to provide incentives to certain types of investments in the economy.
Then they come to this conclusion:
For assets acquired after November 12, 1981 taxpayers will be permitted to claim only one-half of the normal full-year's capital cost allowance in the year of acquisition.
They, the bureaucrats did not know what was going on in the agricultural industry when the Minister of Finance came to that conclusion. They say the rates are deliberately set. You can only take depreciation in accordance with the rates which the Department of Revenue permits. The rates are there on the back page of the farmers' income tax guide. If you use one percentage point more than what they say, the people in the Department of National Revenue correct your income tax. How can the Minister of Finance say that some of these are being depreciated at much faster rates than is warranted? They can only be depreciated at the rates that are allowed by the Department of National Revenue. How can he say that some of these rates are deliberately set in excess of economic depreciation? They can only be applied as granted and permitted by the Department of National Revenue.
Now, let us look at whether this is sensible and reasonable, at whether, as one of the hon. members opposite said the other night, it will hurt anyone if he only gets half the depreciation the first year because he can get the rest later on. I say he
January 28, 1982

might not be alive later on. He needs it now in the same way he has always had it.
Let us look at a drawn combine. You can depreciate that at 10 per cent a year. That means ten years before you can depreciate the purchase price. It is little enough, but it helps to buy a combine. Now, who uses his combine for more than ten years? Advances in technology make it necessary to buy a new combine earlier than that. If you are working a lot of land, you are going to need one before ten years. Is that too fast? It is just being sensible. subtopic: FARM CREDIT ACT FARM LOANS INTEREST REBATE ACT
